findings: Regulatory context. The B Team's own site claims Agentic AI Development, Workflow Automations and AI Company Upgrade services, so EU AI regulation is part of the operating context when work is placed on, used in, or affects people in the EU (https://thebteam.com/services; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers).

Regulatory context. The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and became generally applicable on 2 August 2026, while prohibited AI practices and AI literacy duties started on 2 February 2025 and general-purpose AI model obligations started on 2 August 2025 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).

Regulatory context. The AI literacy duty applies to providers and deployers of AI systems, and Commission Q&A says Article 4 already applies from 2 February 2025 with supervision and enforcement rules applying from August 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers).

Regulatory context. AI Act Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026 to certain generative and interactive AI systems and deepfakes, including duties to inform people when they interact directly with an AI system and to mark AI-generated or manipulated content (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-transparency-obligations).

Regulatory context. High-risk AI classification is not established for The B Team, but the Commission says high-risk areas include biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, migration, asylum and border control, with rules applying from 2 December 2027 for those areas and 2 August 2028 for regulated products (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems).

Regulatory context. Clutch reports a verified The B Team project involving facial-recognition photo features and Azure, so future public claims around biometric or image AI should be screened carefully instead of treated as ordinary web development proof (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems).

Regulatory context. GDPR applies to small and medium-sized enterprises that process personal data, with some obligations depending on whether processing is core to the business or likely to create risk for individuals (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/data-protection-explained_en).

Regulatory context. The European Commission says Standard Contractual Clauses can be used as a GDPR safeguard for transfers from the EU or EEA to third countries, which is material because The B Team serves both U.S. and European clients (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/standard-contractual-clauses-scc_en; https://thebteam.com/).

Regulatory context. The EU Data Act has applied since 12 September 2025, adding buyer context for data access, use and cloud contracts even where a small custom-development vendor is not the main regulated platform (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-act).

Regulatory context. Bulgaria amended its Cybersecurity Act on 13 February 2026 to transpose NIS2, with expanded scope, cybersecurity risk measures, supply-chain security, training, and incident reporting at 24 hours, 72 hours and one month for covered entities (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).

ESG context. The supplied brief marks ESG and Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive context as not applicable for this small private B2B services firm, so direct reporting duties are not established from the supplied material (bteam-blank-slate-brief.md).

ESG context. EU sustainability reporting still matters as buyer context because EU law requires companies above size thresholds to disclose social and environmental risks, opportunities and impacts, and first Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive reports started for financial year 2024 reports published in 2025 (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/financial-markets/company-reporting-and-auditing/company-reporting/corporate-sustainability-reporting_en).

ESG context. The European Commission's 2025 simplification proposal sought to focus Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive duties on companies with more than 1000 employees, which points away from direct scope for a firm publicly described as 10-49, 30 worldwide or 51-200 depending on source (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/financial-markets/company-reporting-and-auditing/company-reporting/corporate-sustainability-reporting_en; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real).

ESG context. EU sustainability due diligence rules entered into force on 25 July 2024 and were later amended, with national measures due by 26 July 2028 and application from 26 July 2029, so direct scope is not shown but larger client supply chains may ask for proof on responsible business conduct (https://commission.europa.eu/topics/business-and-industry/company-law-and-corporate-governance/corporate-sustainability-due-diligence_en).

ESG context. AI claims carry environmental context because the European Commission says data centres use about 1.5 percent of global yearly electricity and that use is projected to more than double by 2030, mainly due to accelerated computing used for AI (https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energy-efficiency-directive/energy-performance-data-centres_en).

Geopolitical context. The B Team's cross-border market is explicit because its site says it is headquartered in Sofia and serves clients across the United States and Europe, and its public contact footprint includes Sofia and Spain (https://thebteam.com/).

Geopolitical context. Bulgaria's position as an EU-based export ICT hub supports The B Team's nearshore story because the U.S. Country Commercial Guide says 70 percent of about 10,000 Bulgarian ICT companies are export-only (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).

Geopolitical context. The World Economic Forum's 2026 Global Risks Report says geoeconomic confrontation was selected as the top risk most likely to trigger a material global crisis in 2026, with state-based armed conflict next, making cross-border buyer trust and continuity proof material for a Bulgaria-based firm serving U.S. and EU clients (https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-risks-report-2026/digest/).

Geopolitical context. The same World Economic Forum report ranks misinformation and disinformation second and cyber insecurity sixth in the two-year outlook, and says adverse outcomes of AI rises from 30th in the two-year outlook to fifth in the 10-year outlook, which makes AI trust claims a live context risk (https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-risks-report-2026/digest/).

Geopolitical context. The European Commission's 2026 Digital Decade country report says Bulgaria has a dynamic ICT sector but that SME uptake of AI, cloud and data analytics remains limited, which gives The B Team an opportunity to stand out but also raises buyer proof expectations (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).

Geopolitical context. The OECD says Bulgaria's AI policy is guided by a 2020 national strategy with pillars including infrastructure, education, research, data, sector innovation and ethical AI, but that the strategy lacks a clear action plan with implementation activities and timelines (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/progress-in-implementing-the-european-union-coordinated-plan-on-artificial-intelligence-volume-1_6d530a88-en/bulgaria_26e81b51-en.html).

Geopolitical context. The OECD also says Bulgaria has Discoverer and HEMUS supercomputing facilities running, Avitohol under development, INSAIT established in 2023, and BgGPT as the country's first open-source Bulgarian-language model, which supports a national AI ecosystem story around Sofia and Bulgaria (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/progress-in-implementing-the-european-union-coordinated-plan-on-artificial-intelligence-volume-1_6d530a88-en/bulgaria_26e81b51-en.html).

Category context. The B Team sits in a crowded Bulgarian software category: the U.S. Country Commercial Guide says Bulgaria has about 10,000 ICT companies, 70 percent of which export, and calls Bulgaria a top ICT outsourcing destination (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).

Category context. The same U.S. guide says Bulgaria's ICT revenue rose 300 percent over seven years to EUR 2.5 billion and that software is the best-performing ICT segment after 16 years of EU membership (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).

Category context. The Manifest lists The B Team among Bulgarian software developers with 8 reviews, a 5.0 rating, 10-49 employees, Sofia location and 2017 establishment, while nearby listings include AI Agents and larger Sofia competitors such as Accedia and Scalefocus (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).

Category context. Clutch lists The B Team at $50-$99 per hour, 10-49 employees, Sofia, founded 2017, and service mix led by 43 percent web development and 15 percent custom software development, which supports the brief's warning that the public profile still reads more like software services than AI specialist (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).

Category context. Clutch independently corroborates delivery proof through a verified Taggable review: a March 2019 ongoing custom software engagement, $50,000 to $199,999 range, about $140,000 spent, Azure and APIs, facial-recognition photo features, and over 1 million photos processed (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).

Category context. H512 describes The B Team Ltd. as a software company serving U.S. clients in finance, retail, healthcare, entertainment and digital communications, with 30 employees worldwide and 20 in Bulgaria, which corroborates the supplied brief's sector range and headcount range (https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/).

Self-description and independent verdict. The B Team's site calls itself "The speed of AI. The soul of craftsmanship." and an "AI development company" in Sofia serving the United States and Europe since 2009; independent directories corroborate Sofia and software delivery but challenge the founding date and stay silent on current agentic AI proof (https://thebteam.com/; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Founding-year conflict. Public history is inconsistent: The B Team says since 2009, H512 says establishment in 2015, LinkedIn and Clutch say founded in 2017, and the Bulgarian registry search result says The B Team Ltd. was new from 6 October 2016 (https://thebteam.com/; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://portal.registryagency.bg/CR/bg/DocumentAccess/MjAzOTEzMzEwJmUmZGJmMjU5ZmM5NmVhNDJhMWJhYjkyYzZkODZkMGM5YWYE8IeWclC2qRaCYJrRADamf8Agz-o9DnMIh84cDNAQ2w). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Ownership history gap. The registry search result reports that Main Assembly Ltd., UIC 204242871, owned 50 shares in The B Team Ltd. on 10 October 2016, but the readable public record did not show later ownership changes or any transaction price (https://portal.registryagency.bg/CR/bg/DocumentAccess/MjAzOTEzMzEwJmUmZGJmMjU5ZmM5NmVhNDJhMWJhYjkyYzZkODZkMGM5YWYE8IeWclC2qRaCYJrRADamf8Agz-o9DnMIh84cDNAQ2w). (bears on: Constraints, guardrails & AI permissions)

Name and search ambiguity. Search ambiguity is material because the public record also surfaces The B Team nonprofit at bteam.org and a separate Atlanta-based B-Team Consulting at b-team.co, while the client's LinkedIn page is named The B Team - Real (https://www.bteam.org/who-we-are/leaders; https://b-team.co/privacy-policy; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Public proof depth. The public The B Team site pages opened for services, process, case studies, lab and news exposed the same short site shell rather than detailed proof assets, so public proof depth remains thin from the opened pages (https://thebteam.com/services; https://thebteam.com/process; https://thebteam.com/case-studies; https://www.thebteam.com/lab; https://thebteam.com/news). (bears on: Baseline data & measurement access)

Regulatory context. The EU Cyber Resilience Act entered into force on 10 December 2024; its main obligations apply from 11 December 2027 and reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act).

Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act applies to software or hardware products with digital elements made available on the EU market, so direct scope for The B Team depends on whether it markets software under its own name or trademark rather than only providing bespoke development services (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).

Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to perform a cybersecurity risk assessment, keep technical documentation, provide support-period information, handle vulnerabilities and run conformity assessment before placing covered products on the EU market (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).

Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act requires actively exploited vulnerability and severe-incident notices through the CRA reporting route, with 24-hour early warning, 72-hour main notice, and later final reports depending on the event (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).

Regulatory context. The Commission's 2026 guidance for general-purpose AI model providers says only significant modifications to AI models trigger provider obligations, while minor modifications do not, so The B Team should distinguish model integration from model-provider activity in any public AI claim (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers).

Regulatory context. The same guidance says Commission enforcement powers for general-purpose AI provider obligations start on 2 August 2026, and providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers).

Regulatory context. The European Data Protection Board's AI-model opinion says anonymity must be assessed case by case, and an AI model is anonymous only where identification or extraction of personal data is very unlikely, which matters for AI projects using client, user or scraped data (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-opinion-on-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en).

Regulatory context. The same EDPB opinion says legitimate interest can support some AI development or deployment only if processing is strictly necessary and the rights-balancing test is met, and unlawfully processed development data can affect later use unless the model has been properly anonymized (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-opinion-on-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en).

Regulatory context. DORA has applied from 17 January 2025 and requires financial entities to manage ICT risk, report incidents, test resilience and govern ICT third-party providers, so The B Team's finance-sector work may face buyer due-diligence demands even if direct DORA designation is not established (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/news/digital-finance-2024-12-19_en).

ESG context. The EU Platform on Sustainable Finance says SMEs account for more than 50 percent of EU GDP and more than 63 percent of enterprise CO2 and wider greenhouse-gas emissions, so even small firms can face sustainability questions from banks, clients and partners (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/0d8e5199-44c2-4a17-affc-0f398443e603_en?filename=250321-sustainable-finance-platform-report-smes_en.pdf).

ESG context. The same report says Taxonomy-related information requests can pass down to SMEs from value-chain partners or clients, so The B Team may need simple climate and energy facts even if direct reporting duties are not established (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/0d8e5199-44c2-4a17-affc-0f398443e603_en?filename=250321-sustainable-finance-platform-report-smes_en.pdf).

ESG context. The same report says more than 90 percent of EU SMEs are taking resource-efficiency measures, 58 percent of surveyed SMEs had invested in sustainability-related improvements, and 65 percent financed those projects themselves, which gives a peer baseline for any claim that The B Team is responsible as a small supplier (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/0d8e5199-44c2-4a17-affc-0f398443e603_en?filename=250321-sustainable-finance-platform-report-smes_en.pdf).

Geopolitical context. The European Commission adopted the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision on 10 July 2023, allowing personal data to flow freely from the EU to participating U.S. companies, which is material to The B Team's U.S. and Europe client base (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/eu-us-data-transfers_en).

Geopolitical context. The Commission published the first review of that adequacy decision on 9 October 2024, so transatlantic data-transfer assurance has an active review history rather than being a settled background assumption (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/adequacy-decisions_en).

Geopolitical context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says the United States had 5,427 AI data centers and that nearly all leading AI chips depend on one Taiwanese foundry, while U.S. AI talent inflow has dropped 89 percent since 2017, making AI supply-chain and talent geography part of the context for an EU-based AI services partner (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).

Geopolitical context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says national AI strategies and state-backed AI supercomputing are rising, but model production remains concentrated in the United States and China, which reinforces the need for a Sofia-based firm to state clearly whether it builds, adapts, integrates or governs third-party models (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).

Category context. Gartner's 2026 agentic-AI cycle says only 17 percent of organizations have deployed AI agents, while more than 60 percent expect to do so within two years, so demand is high but proof of real delivery is still scarce (https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/hype-cycle-for-agentic-ai).

Category context. Gartner says agentic AI is at the "Peak of Inflated Expectations" and that fully autonomous agents are not ready for most enterprise uses, which makes an unqualified AI-agent claim risky for a small vendor with thin public proof (https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/hype-cycle-for-agentic-ai).

Category context. Gartner predicted in August 2025 that 40 percent of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5 percent at the time, which supports The B Team's AI-market opportunity (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-08-26-gartner-predicts-40-percent-of-enterprise-apps-will-feature-task-specific-ai-agents-by-2026-up-from-less-than-5-percent-in-2025).

Category context. Gartner also predicts that by 2027, 40 percent of enterprises will demote or shut down autonomous AI agents because governance gaps are found only after production incidents, so The B Team's category proof should cover autonomy level, access limits, approvals, logs, rollback and ownership (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-26-gartner-says-applying-uniform-governance-across-ai-agents-will-lead-to-enterprise-ai-agent-failure).

Category context. McKinsey's 2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey says only about 30 percent of organizations reach maturity level three or higher in strategy, governance and agentic-AI controls, which makes trust architecture a buyer concern rather than a legal footnote (https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/tech-forward/state-of-ai-trust-in-2026-shifting-to-the-agentic-era).

Category context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says organizational AI adoption reached 88 percent, SWE-bench Verified coding performance rose from 60 percent to near 100 percent in one year, and AI agents improved from 12 percent to about 66 percent task success on OSWorld while still failing about one in three attempts, which frames both the opportunity and the reliability gap in The B Team's market (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).

2022 rebrand marker. A connected Main Assembly news item says on 18 October 2022 that it congratulated The B Team for a "rebranding and website launch", which adds a public marker for when the current brand story changed (https://www.mainassembly.com/news/2022/10/18/congratulations-the-b-team). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Connected founder-investor record. Main Assembly says Matthew Maday lists The B Team as "Co-Founder and Investor", while the banked Bulgarian registry finding says Main Assembly Ltd. held 50 shares in The B Team Ltd. on 10 October 2016; the opened record still does not establish later ownership changes or any transaction price (https://www.mainassembly.com/leadership; banked finding: Ownership history gap). (bears on: Constraints, guardrails & AI permissions)

Related-company model. Main Assembly describes its model as "development for ownership" and says it offers free development services and executive support to companies it works with; the banked registry finding corroborates a formal ownership link at The B Team's start, but the opened public sources did not show how that model applies to The B Team today (https://www.mainassembly.com/what-we-do; banked finding: Ownership history gap). (bears on: Business problem / organizational objective)

Pattern across banked findings. The banked record now shows one clear pattern: The B Team is trying to move from a crowded Sofia software-services market into AI while EU AI rules, GDPR, data-transfer rules, AI energy concerns, geopolitical risk and agentic-AI buyer caution all make proof of safe delivery part of the reputation problem (banked findings: Regulatory context, ESG context, Geopolitical context, Category context, Self-description and independent verdict, Public proof depth). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Regulatory context. The new EU Product Liability Directive entered into force on 8 December 2024, must be transposed by EU countries by 9 December 2026, and applies to products placed on the EU market from 9 December 2026. It is built for new technologies including artificial intelligence and covers damage including destruction or corruption of data, so The B Team should separate bespoke services from any software or AI product it places on the EU market (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/free-movement-sectors/liability-defective-products_en).

Regulatory context. The same EU Product Liability Directive seeks to ensure there is an EU-based liable party even where the manufacturer is outside the EU. This matters for The B Team's U.S.-Europe work because any claim about ownership, deployment, resale or support of AI software may affect who is treated as the liable economic operator (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/free-movement-sectors/liability-defective-products_en).

draft.hypothesis: The B Team's reputation problem is not weak capability; it is that the public proof system has not caught up with the AI-era story the company now wants buyers to believe. The white space is a proof-first AI software partner that shows exactly where its AI claim is true, where its public record still proves enterprise software craft better than AI depth, and where larger peers compete through scale and broader proof libraries. The strategy should first make the company easier to trust, then make it more visible. must_avoid: Do not overstate AI capability, certifications, client wins or metrics.
Do not invent client names, case studies, project specifics or proof points.
Do not rely on generic nearshore claims as the central idea.
Do not ignore public-source inconsistencies.

expected_outputs: Corporate reputation platform and message architecture
Measurement framework aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework
success_criteria: Checks readiness and identifies gaps before strategy writing starts.
Resists inventing proof where evidence is thin.
Shows positioning options before recommendation.
Separates facts, missing inputs, conflicting signals and strategic judgment.
Produces a lean strategy a founder-led small team can run.
Makes the message architecture and proof model the first client-facing decision artifact.

do_not_say: Do not say The B Team is a proven agentic AI leader unless named or verifiable proof supports it.
Do not claim AI certifications unless the client provides evidence.
Do not invent client names, project specifics, metrics or case studies.
Do not use founding-year or headcount claims until the client reconciles the public record.
Do not make generic nearshore-cost claims the central idea.
claim_rules: Separate public fact, client-supplied claim, conflicting signal, gap and strategic judgment.
Use AI claims only inside the proof boundary the evidence supports.
Mark client-owned claims as owner-published unless an independent source corroborates them.
Use public client names only where they are already public and relevant.
Treat hypotheses as provisional until client evidence confirms or overturns them.

legal: General Data Protection Regulation and US data expectations apply to marketing data and claims about client data handling.
Capability claims must be accurate because overstated AI capability or certifications create commercial and trust risk.
confidentiality: Most B2B software work is under non-disclosure agreements, so named case studies require client permission.
The desk audit may use public sources, but the deliverable must not expose non-public client names, contract terms, project specifics, internal financials or employee details below founder level.
ai_use: Use only publicly available information plus the supplied brief.
Exclude non-public client names, contract terms, project specifics, internal financials and individual employee details below founder level.
Where public facts conflict, flag the inconsistency instead of choosing one and asserting it.
Do not invent proof, clients, metrics or AI capabilities.
anonymization: The supplied demo masking of the company and founders is retired because this run declares the client as The B Team and names the founders where public sources support it.
Non-public client names and project details remain masked as sector descriptors.
Exact non-public financials and headcount stay generalized, while public financial and headcount records may be cited as public-source evidence.

founder_ambition_and_constraints: The founders must decide whether the company leads with AI-era specialist positioning, craft-led senior engineering, founder-led trust or proof-first credibility building.
The two founders may weight craftsmanship and AI-forward emphasis differently.
Limited marketing capacity constrains the strategy to lean, founder-doable moves.
small_team_execution_framing: The strategy must be executable by a founder-led small team.
Proof-building should come before broad earned-media activity.
The roadmap should use low-overhead owned, shared, referral and proof-library moves before heavier campaigns.
early_name_and_search_discoverability: The public record shows name ambiguity with other The B Team entities.
The public record shows domain and identity split across thebteam.com, yourbteam.com and other indexed signals.

# What we need from you on the Pre-Engagement Briefing Pack

The AI (artificial intelligence) desk audit is done and the pack is drafted. These are the calls the method keeps for a person. Nothing after this step runs until the point of view on the hypothesis and the style calibration each carry an answer with your name against it.

How to answer: under each section write `Approved by: <name>` if the draft stands, or `Changed by: <name>` and what it should say instead. Both are decisions; only an approval settles a section.

Blocking the rest of the work: the point of view on the hypothesis, and the style calibration.

Not blocking: the question bank. The method drafts it here and tailors it during the later client-intake work, so it travels on as a draft. Say what you would change if you want it changed now; the run does not wait on it.

## How to use this review

Terms, context and next steps orient the reader.

### Terms

- Approved by — the operator's mark on a numbered section that the draft in it stands as written
- Changed by — the operator's mark on a numbered section that the draft in it is being replaced, followed by what it should say instead
- section — one of the numbered blocks below, each covering one part of the pre-engagement briefing pack the review is built from
- guided interview — the sequenced-prompt review mode the operator can choose instead of this page; the same content asked one section at a time

### Context

This is the operator-review page for the pre-engagement briefing pack. It travels with the pack as the second thing Phases 2 and 3 produce, and it lists the questions the operator has to answer before anything downstream advances.

### Next steps

Under each numbered section below, write `Approved by: <name>` if the draft stands, or `Changed by: <name>` and what it should say instead. Both are decisions; only an approval settles a section. Nothing after Phase 3 runs until the point of view on the hypothesis and the style calibration each carry an approved answer with a name against it. The question bank is recorded here and tailored in step two, so it does not hold the run.

## 1. Business Audit

Read the Business audit findings and gaps below. Do the findings hold up on the client you know, and is any gap the one that would change how you walk into the client conversation?

*Findings as drafted:*

findings: What the company does. The company self-description includes an unreconciled founding-year claim: it says it has delivered enterprise-grade software engineering, AI-powered automation and architect-led delivery since 2009, but this should not be used as a buyer-facing fact until the founders settle the date; buyer-facing materials should instead lean on the senior team and 20+ years' experience supported by founder bios (https://thebteam.com/).

What the company does. That self-description is partly corroborated and partly challenged: H512 corroborates software and hardware product development for US clients, Clutch corroborates software, web, ERP, medical technology and mobile app work, and Bulgarian records challenge the 2009 company-date claim by showing registration on 9 February 2016; treat the founding year as an unreconciled claim, not a buyer-facing fact, and keep it out of buyer-facing materials until the founders settle it (https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://papagal.bg/eik/203913310/d653).
What the company does. The current company site lists services as Hand-Crafted Development, Agentic AI Development, Workflow Automations and AI Company Upgrade (https://thebteam.com/services).

What the company does. H512 says The B Team Ltd. develops and maintains software and hardware products, and identifies its activity as product company and software systems implementation (https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/).
What the company does. Clutch describes The B Team as a provider of websites, ERP systems, medical technologies and mobile apps (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).

What the company does. The Manifest describes The B Team as a web development company founded in 2017 and lists web development, custom software development, web design and e-commerce development (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).
What the company does. Company Guru classifies the legal entity's industry as computer programming (https://web.company.guru/203913310).

Its business model. The supplied brief says the firm sells senior engineering capability to companies, not consumers, through custom and enterprise software, AI-powered automation and agentic AI development (bteam-blank-slate-brief.md).

Its business model. The company site says it serves clients in the United States and Europe with senior AI developers and a PMP-structured delivery model; independent sources corroborate US and Europe-facing software services, but not the full AI claim (https://thebteam.com/; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).
Its business model. Clutch lists an average hourly rate of $50 to $99 per hour, an undisclosed minimum project size and 10 to 49 employees (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).

Its business model. Clutch says the most common project size is $50,000 to $199,999 based on seven reviews, and its pricing summary says reviewed project investments ranged from $68,000 to $1 million (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).
Its business model. Clutch classifies the client mix as 60% enterprise, 20% midmarket and 20% small business (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).
Its business model. H512 says the company works with US clients across finance, retail, healthcare, entertainment, digital communications and other segments (https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/).

Its business model. Agency Spotter describes the firm as a website and mobile app development company serving startups, manufacturers, medical technologies, commerce solutions and corporate websites (https://www.agencyspotter.com/the-b-team).

Its business model. The company register activity is much broader than the operating profile; Company Guru classifies the industry as computer programming, while the registered object also includes representation, intellectual property transactions, property, agriculture, transport, investment, hotels, tourism and restaurants (https://web.company.guru/203913310; https://companybook.bg/companies/203913310).

findings: Regulatory context. The B Team's own site claims Agentic AI Development, Workflow Automations and AI Company Upgrade services, so EU AI regulation is part of the operating context when work is placed on, used in, or affects people in the EU (https://thebteam.com/services; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers).

Regulatory context. The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and became generally applicable on 2 August 2026, while prohibited AI practices and AI literacy duties started on 2 February 2025 and general-purpose AI model obligations started on 2 August 2025 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).

Regulatory context. The AI literacy duty applies to providers and deployers of AI systems, and Commission Q&A says Article 4 already applies from 2 February 2025 with supervision and enforcement rules applying from August 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers).

Regulatory context. AI Act Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026 to certain generative and interactive AI systems and deepfakes, including duties to inform people when they interact directly with an AI system and to mark AI-generated or manipulated content (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-transparency-obligations).

Regulatory context. High-risk AI classification is not established for The B Team, but the Commission says high-risk areas include biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, migration, asylum and border control, with rules applying from 2 December 2027 for those areas and 2 August 2028 for regulated products (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems).

Regulatory context. Clutch reports a verified The B Team project involving facial-recognition photo features and Azure, so future public claims around biometric or image AI should be screened carefully instead of treated as ordinary web development proof (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems).

Regulatory context. GDPR applies to small and medium-sized enterprises that process personal data, with some obligations depending on whether processing is core to the business or likely to create risk for individuals (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/data-protection-explained_en).

Regulatory context. The European Commission says Standard Contractual Clauses can be used as a GDPR safeguard for transfers from the EU or EEA to third countries, which is material because The B Team serves both U.S. and European clients (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/standard-contractual-clauses-scc_en; https://thebteam.com/).

Regulatory context. The EU Data Act has applied since 12 September 2025, adding buyer context for data access, use and cloud contracts even where a small custom-development vendor is not the main regulated platform (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-act).

Regulatory context. Bulgaria amended its Cybersecurity Act on 13 February 2026 to transpose NIS2, with expanded scope, cybersecurity risk measures, supply-chain security, training, and incident reporting at 24 hours, 72 hours and one month for covered entities (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).

ESG context. The supplied brief marks ESG and Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive context as not applicable for this small private B2B services firm, so direct reporting duties are not established from the supplied material (bteam-blank-slate-brief.md).

ESG context. EU sustainability reporting still matters as buyer context because EU law requires companies above size thresholds to disclose social and environmental risks, opportunities and impacts, and first Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive reports started for financial year 2024 reports published in 2025 (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/financial-markets/company-reporting-and-auditing/company-reporting/corporate-sustainability-reporting_en).

ESG context. The European Commission's 2025 simplification proposal sought to focus Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive duties on companies with more than 1000 employees, which points away from direct scope for a firm publicly described as 10-49, 30 worldwide or 51-200 depending on source (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/financial-markets/company-reporting-and-auditing/company-reporting/corporate-sustainability-reporting_en; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real).

ESG context. EU sustainability due diligence rules entered into force on 25 July 2024 and were later amended, with national measures due by 26 July 2028 and application from 26 July 2029, so direct scope is not shown but larger client supply chains may ask for proof on responsible business conduct (https://commission.europa.eu/topics/business-and-industry/company-law-and-corporate-governance/corporate-sustainability-due-diligence_en).

ESG context. AI claims carry environmental context because the European Commission says data centres use about 1.5 percent of global yearly electricity and that use is projected to more than double by 2030, mainly due to accelerated computing used for AI (https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energy-efficiency-directive/energy-performance-data-centres_en).

Geopolitical context. The B Team's cross-border market is explicit because its site says it is headquartered in Sofia and serves clients across the United States and Europe, and its public contact footprint includes Sofia and Spain (https://thebteam.com/).

Geopolitical context. Bulgaria's position as an EU-based export ICT hub supports The B Team's nearshore story because the U.S. Country Commercial Guide says 70 percent of about 10,000 Bulgarian ICT companies are export-only (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).

Geopolitical context. The World Economic Forum's 2026 Global Risks Report says geoeconomic confrontation was selected as the top risk most likely to trigger a material global crisis in 2026, with state-based armed conflict next, making cross-border buyer trust and continuity proof material for a Bulgaria-based firm serving U.S. and EU clients (https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-risks-report-2026/digest/).

Geopolitical context. The same World Economic Forum report ranks misinformation and disinformation second and cyber insecurity sixth in the two-year outlook, and says adverse outcomes of AI rises from 30th in the two-year outlook to fifth in the 10-year outlook, which makes AI trust claims a live context risk (https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-risks-report-2026/digest/).

Geopolitical context. The European Commission's 2026 Digital Decade country report says Bulgaria has a dynamic ICT sector but that SME uptake of AI, cloud and data analytics remains limited, which gives The B Team an opportunity to stand out but also raises buyer proof expectations (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).

Geopolitical context. The OECD says Bulgaria's AI policy is guided by a 2020 national strategy with pillars including infrastructure, education, research, data, sector innovation and ethical AI, but that the strategy lacks a clear action plan with implementation activities and timelines (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/progress-in-implementing-the-european-union-coordinated-plan-on-artificial-intelligence-volume-1_6d530a88-en/bulgaria_26e81b51-en.html).

Geopolitical context. The OECD also says Bulgaria has Discoverer and HEMUS supercomputing facilities running, Avitohol under development, INSAIT established in 2023, and BgGPT as the country's first open-source Bulgarian-language model, which supports a national AI ecosystem story around Sofia and Bulgaria (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/progress-in-implementing-the-european-union-coordinated-plan-on-artificial-intelligence-volume-1_6d530a88-en/bulgaria_26e81b51-en.html).

Category context. The B Team sits in a crowded Bulgarian software category: the U.S. Country Commercial Guide says Bulgaria has about 10,000 ICT companies, 70 percent of which export, and calls Bulgaria a top ICT outsourcing destination (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).

Category context. The same U.S. guide says Bulgaria's ICT revenue rose 300 percent over seven years to EUR 2.5 billion and that software is the best-performing ICT segment after 16 years of EU membership (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).

Category context. The Manifest lists The B Team among Bulgarian software developers with 8 reviews, a 5.0 rating, 10-49 employees, Sofia location and 2017 establishment, while nearby listings include AI Agents and larger Sofia competitors such as Accedia and Scalefocus (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).

Category context. Clutch lists The B Team at $50-$99 per hour, 10-49 employees, Sofia, founded 2017, and service mix led by 43 percent web development and 15 percent custom software development, which supports the brief's warning that the public profile still reads more like software services than AI specialist (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).

Category context. Clutch independently corroborates delivery proof through a verified Taggable review: a March 2019 ongoing custom software engagement, $50,000 to $199,999 range, about $140,000 spent, Azure and APIs, facial-recognition photo features, and over 1 million photos processed (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).

Category context. H512 describes The B Team Ltd. as a software company serving U.S. clients in finance, retail, healthcare, entertainment and digital communications, with 30 employees worldwide and 20 in Bulgaria, which corroborates the supplied brief's sector range and headcount range (https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/).

The soul of craftsmanship." and an "AI development company" in Sofia serving the United States and Europe since 2009; independent directories corroborate Sofia and software delivery but challenge the founding date and stay silent on current agentic AI proof (https://thebteam.com/; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real). (bears on: Baseline data & measurement access)

Regulatory context. The EU Cyber Resilience Act entered into force on 10 December 2024; its main obligations apply from 11 December 2027 and reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act).

Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act applies to software or hardware products with digital elements made available on the EU market, so direct scope for The B Team depends on whether it markets software under its own name or trademark rather than only providing bespoke development services (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).

Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to perform a cybersecurity risk assessment, keep technical documentation, provide support-period information, handle vulnerabilities and run conformity assessment before placing covered products on the EU market (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).

Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act requires actively exploited vulnerability and severe-incident notices through the CRA reporting route, with 24-hour early warning, 72-hour main notice, and later final reports depending on the event (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).

Regulatory context. The Commission's 2026 guidance for general-purpose AI model providers says only significant modifications to AI models trigger provider obligations, while minor modifications do not, so The B Team should distinguish model integration from model-provider activity in any public AI claim (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers).

Regulatory context. The same guidance says Commission enforcement powers for general-purpose AI provider obligations start on 2 August 2026, and providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers).

Regulatory context. The European Data Protection Board's AI-model opinion says anonymity must be assessed case by case, and an AI model is anonymous only where identification or extraction of personal data is very unlikely, which matters for AI projects using client, user or scraped data (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-opinion-on-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en).

Regulatory context. The same EDPB opinion says legitimate interest can support some AI development or deployment only if processing is strictly necessary and the rights-balancing test is met, and unlawfully processed development data can affect later use unless the model has been properly anonymized (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-opinion-on-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en).

Regulatory context. DORA has applied from 17 January 2025 and requires financial entities to manage ICT risk, report incidents, test resilience and govern ICT third-party providers, so The B Team's finance-sector work may face buyer due-diligence demands even if direct DORA designation is not established (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/news/digital-finance-2024-12-19_en).

ESG context. The EU Platform on Sustainable Finance says SMEs account for more than 50 percent of EU GDP and more than 63 percent of enterprise CO2 and wider greenhouse-gas emissions, so even small firms can face sustainability questions from banks, clients and partners (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/0d8e5199-44c2-4a17-affc-0f398443e603_en?filename=250321-sustainable-finance-platform-report-smes_en.pdf).

ESG context. The same report says Taxonomy-related information requests can pass down to SMEs from value-chain partners or clients, so The B Team may need simple climate and energy facts even if direct reporting duties are not established (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/0d8e5199-44c2-4a17-affc-0f398443e603_en?filename=250321-sustainable-finance-platform-report-smes_en.pdf).

ESG context. The same report says more than 90 percent of EU SMEs are taking resource-efficiency measures, 58 percent of surveyed SMEs had invested in sustainability-related improvements, and 65 percent financed those projects themselves, which gives a peer baseline for any claim that The B Team is responsible as a small supplier (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/0d8e5199-44c2-4a17-affc-0f398443e603_en?filename=250321-sustainable-finance-platform-report-smes_en.pdf).

Geopolitical context. The European Commission adopted the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision on 10 July 2023, allowing personal data to flow freely from the EU to participating U.S. companies, which is material to The B Team's U.S. and Europe client base (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/eu-us-data-transfers_en).

Geopolitical context. The Commission published the first review of that adequacy decision on 9 October 2024, so transatlantic data-transfer assurance has an active review history rather than being a settled background assumption (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/adequacy-decisions_en).

Geopolitical context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says the United States had 5,427 AI data centers and that nearly all leading AI chips depend on one Taiwanese foundry, while U.S. AI talent inflow has dropped 89 percent since 2017, making AI supply-chain and talent geography part of the context for an EU-based AI services partner (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).

Geopolitical context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says national AI strategies and state-backed AI supercomputing are rising, but model production remains concentrated in the United States and China, which reinforces the need for a Sofia-based firm to state clearly whether it builds, adapts, integrates or governs third-party models (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).

Category context. Gartner's 2026 agentic-AI cycle says only 17 percent of organizations have deployed AI agents, while more than 60 percent expect to do so within two years, so demand is high but proof of real delivery is still scarce (https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/hype-cycle-for-agentic-ai).

Category context. Gartner says agentic AI is at the "Peak of Inflated Expectations" and that fully autonomous agents are not ready for most enterprise uses, which makes an unqualified AI-agent claim risky for a small vendor with thin public proof (https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/hype-cycle-for-agentic-ai).

Category context. Gartner predicted in August 2025 that 40 percent of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5 percent at the time, which supports The B Team's AI-market opportunity (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-08-26-gartner-predicts-40-percent-of-enterprise-apps-will-feature-task-specific-ai-agents-by-2026-up-from-less-than-5-percent-in-2025).

Category context. Gartner also predicts that by 2027, 40 percent of enterprises will demote or shut down autonomous AI agents because governance gaps are found only after production incidents, so The B Team's category proof should cover autonomy level, access limits, approvals, logs, rollback and ownership (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-26-gartner-says-applying-uniform-governance-across-ai-agents-will-lead-to-enterprise-ai-agent-failure).

Category context. McKinsey's 2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey says only about 30 percent of organizations reach maturity level three or higher in strategy, governance and agentic-AI controls, which makes trust architecture a buyer concern rather than a legal footnote (https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/tech-forward/state-of-ai-trust-in-2026-shifting-to-the-agentic-era).

Category context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says organizational AI adoption reached 88 percent, SWE-bench Verified coding performance rose from 60 percent to near 100 percent in one year, and AI agents improved from 12 percent to about 66 percent task success on OSWorld while still failing about one in three attempts, which frames both the opportunity and the reliability gap in The B Team's market (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).

2022 rebrand marker. A connected Main Assembly news item says on 18 October 2022 that it congratulated The B Team for a "rebranding and website launch", which adds a public marker for when the current brand story changed (https://www.mainassembly.com/news/2022/10/18/congratulations-the-b-team). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Connected founder-investor record. Main Assembly says Matthew Maday lists The B Team as "Co-Founder and Investor", while the banked Bulgarian registry finding says Main Assembly Ltd. held 50 shares in The B Team Ltd. on 10 October 2016; the opened record still does not establish later ownership changes or any transaction price (https://www.mainassembly.com/leadership; banked finding: Ownership history gap). (bears on: Constraints, guardrails & AI permissions)

Related-company model. Main Assembly describes its model as "development for ownership" and says it offers free development services and executive support to companies it works with; the banked registry finding corroborates a formal ownership link at The B Team's start, but the opened public sources did not show how that model applies to The B Team today (https://www.mainassembly.com/what-we-do; banked finding: Ownership history gap). (bears on: Business problem / organizational objective)

Pattern across banked findings. The banked record now shows one clear pattern: The B Team is trying to move from a crowded Sofia software-services market into AI while EU AI rules, GDPR, data-transfer rules, AI energy concerns, geopolitical risk and agentic-AI buyer caution all make proof of safe delivery part of the reputation problem (banked findings: Regulatory context, ESG context, Geopolitical context, Category context, Self-description and independent verdict, Public proof depth). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Regulatory context. The new EU Product Liability Directive entered into force on 8 December 2024, must be transposed by EU countries by 9 December 2026, and applies to products placed on the EU market from 9 December 2026. It is built for new technologies including artificial intelligence and covers damage including destruction or corruption of data, so The B Team should separate bespoke services from any software or AI product it places on the EU market (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/free-movement-sectors/liability-defective-products_en).

Regulatory context. The same EU Product Liability Directive seeks to ensure there is an EU-based liable party even where the manufacturer is outside the EU. This matters for The B Team's U.S.-Europe work because any claim about ownership, deployment, resale or support of AI software may affect who is treated as the liable economic operator (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/free-movement-sectors/liability-defective-products_en).

Regulatory context. The European Commission says a company using a third-party contact list for direct marketing must be able to show GDPR-compliant collection, respect objections, inform people at first contact, and comply with ePrivacy rules for email marketing. This is material to a proof-building plan that may use founder outreach, referral lists, events or CRM exports (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/information-business-and-organisations/legal-grounds-processing-data/can-data-received-third-party-be-used-marketing_en).

Regulatory context. The FTC says advertising claims must be truthful, not deceptive or unfair, and evidence-based, including for online advertising that sells software, apps or other services. This adds U.S. claim-risk context to The B Team's AI-forward message for U.S. buyers (https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing).

Regulatory context. The FTC says model-as-a-service companies may be liable if they break privacy commitments, including promises not to use customer data to train or update models through direct or indirect methods. This is relevant even if The B Team integrates third-party models, because U.S. buyers may ask how client data, prompts and outputs are handled across providers (https://www.ftc.gov/policy/advocacy-research/tech-at-ftc/2024/01/ai-companies-uphold-your-privacy-confidentiality-commitments).

Regulatory context. The B Team privacy-policy search result says, "We do not use your personal data for automated decision-making or profiling" with legal or similar significant effects. Independent public sources opened in this pass stayed silent on that claim, and the opened page did not expose a detailed data-processing agreement, subprocessor list or AI-data-use terms (https://thebteam.com/privacy-policy).

Regulatory context. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary and is meant to help organizations build trustworthiness into the design, development, use and evaluation of AI products, services and systems. final_pre_engagement_pack_content.hypothesis: The B Team's reputation problem is not weak capability; it is that the public proof system has not caught up with the AI-era story the company now wants buyers to believe. The white space is a proof-first AI software partner that shows exactly where its AI claim is true, where its public record still proves enterprise software craft better than AI depth, and where larger peers compete through scale and broader proof libraries. The strategy should make identity consolidation the first move, so the company becomes easier to trust before it becomes more visible. (rests on: AI proof gap) (rests on: Positioning-history pattern) (rests on: Each peer's share of voice) (rests on: Public identity pattern)

hypothesis_test.confirms: The hypothesis holds if client-approved proof shows shipped AI or automation work, named or anonymous but verifiable references, and a public proof library that connects the AI offer to existing enterprise software evidence.
hypothesis_test.overturns: The hypothesis is wrong if further research shows buyers already recognize The B Team as an AI specialist, the current AI claim is independently proven across recent work, and public inconsistency is not affecting trust or discovery.

style_note.sentence_length: Sentences are mostly short to medium, with one clear claim per line or paragraph.
style_note.vocabulary: The vocabulary combines engineering terms with human delivery language: AI development, enterprise-grade software, automation, architect-led delivery, craft, workflow and fit.
style_note.self_reference: The client refers to itself as The B Team and uses first-person plural sparingly through service and contact language.

# CD-S-002 Client Leadership Interview — Canonical Question Set

Canonical, harness-owned client-leadership interview question set for CD-S-002 corporate
communications strategy. Organized on the Purpose -> Proof -> Positioning -> Priorities ->
Risks -> Future arc. The interview-ingestion phase maps each respondent answer to one of
these questions by its exact text; the deterministic gate validates every extracted prompt
against this set. Override per engagement via inputs["interview_question_set_path"] or inline
inputs["interview_question_set"].

## Part 1 — Purpose
1. Beyond the products and services we sell… Why does the company matter? Where did the company come from, and what were its founders trying to change?
2. Imagine the company disappeared tomorrow. What would genuinely be missed?
3. What contribution over the last few years makes you personally proud?
4. If you had to describe the company in one sentence to someone who knows nothing about it, what would you say?
5. What do people still not understand about the company?
6. As the company enters a new leadership chapter… What should stay exactly the same? What should change?

## Part 2 — Proof
7. Which achievement best proves what the company stands for?
8. How would you prove it? What facts, numbers or examples give you confidence?
9. If someone challenged that achievement tomorrow, would the evidence be strong enough? Why?
10. Where do we already have strong proof? Where are we still ahead of the evidence?
11. What's one success story that deserves far more attention than it gets today?

## Part 3 — Positioning
12. Lots of companies say they're innovative, trusted and customer-focused. What makes this company genuinely different?
13. What's something only this company can honestly say?
14. What should the company stop saying about itself?
15. What should the company never become?
16. When people hear the company's name… What do you hope comes to mind first?

## Part 4 — Priorities
17. If only one group had to believe our story first… Who would it be? Why?
18. Which audience is hardest to convince today? Why?
19. Inside the company… Where do leaders see the future differently?
20. What would help everyone inside the company tell the same story?

## Part 5 — Risks
21. Which claims make you uncomfortable because we haven't fully earned them yet?
22. What topics require extra care before speaking publicly?
23. If you worked for a competitor… What weakness would you attack first?
24. Where do our actions still fall short of our ambitions?
25. What issue from the past could still shape how people see us today?

## Part 6 — The Future
26. Three years from now… What do you hope people say about the company?
27. What decisions do we need to make this year to earn that reputation?
28. How bold should our story be? Too cautious has risks. Too ambitious has risks. Where is the right balance?
29. Beyond reputation… How will we know we've succeeded?
30. If you could change just one thing about how the company is perceived tomorrow morning… What would it be?

## Closer
31. What question should I have asked — but didn't?

# Client Intake Brief

The B Team · Step 3 Final Brief. This brief defines the task the strategy is built from. It takes effect only when the named decision-maker approves it in writing, and no work begins before that.

## Client & context

_Who they are, business model, markets, moment._

The B Team is a small, founder-led business-to-business software engineering firm based in Sofia, serving buyers in the United States and Europe. It is repositioning from offshore and nearshore software services toward artificial intelligence (AI) development and agentic AI. Its public record still proves enterprise software delivery more strongly than its current AI depth.

## Organisational objective

_The business change and by when; the story change that delivers it._

Business objective. Win two qualified enterprise leads a quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union, reached by the second quarter of 2027. Kamen Kamenov set this commercial target in writing on 25 August 2026. Communications objective. Move the company’s story from a nearshore software-services perception to a proof-led AI engineering partner — built on governed AI, senior craft and outcome ownership.

## Assignment — the deliverable

_What the strategy work produces, which discipline leads, and how far the scope runs._

Deliverable. An integrated brand-and-corporate communications strategy, delivered as a complete document. Lead discipline. Corporate-led — the core problem is reputation and credibility (proving a newer AI story), so the corporate/reputation strategy leads and the brand and demand work (positioning, consideration, founder visibility, lead generation) sits beneath it and serves it. For a founder-led SME the two are closely fused; this brief names which leads so the strategy does not split into two disconnected halves. Scope. Strategy is the Step 3 deliverable — situation analysis, audience and proof strategy, positioning and narrative, message architecture, channel approach and measurement. Creative platform, production and activation are a named later phase, not part of this deliverable, and are costed separately when the pilot moves beyond internal cost.

## Reputation problem / opportunity

_Current perception versus desired; the misperception to close._

The B Team is asking buyers to believe a newer AI story before its public proof fully supports it. There is a gap between the owned line — “The speed of AI. The soul of craftsmanship” — and third-party records that still describe mainly web, software and offshore delivery. Public sources also carry inconsistent signals on founding year, headcount, address and legal name.

## Priority audiences

_Segments and their current state: what they know, feel and do today._

The audience order is settled. Kamen Kamenov decided in writing on 24 August 2026 that owners of midsize businesses lead as the primary audience — particularly those who want more control and visibility through the harness approach. Technical buyers, chiefly CTOs and the people who own the architecture, follow as the audience the proof has to win over, on Matthew’s standard that they are the hardest to convince. Senior Sofia talent is the third audience.

## Desired change

_What each audience must know, feel or do differently._

Technical buyers need to see enough proof to trust the governed-AI claim, not just the language around it. Midsize business owners need to understand that the harness gives them more control and visibility. Senior Sofia engineers need to see that AI supports better architectural work rather than replacing craft.

## Stakeholders & internal alignment

_Key internal players, their wants and fears, and the conflicts between them._

Both founders agree the governed harness sits at the centre of the story, but they differ on launch order and first audience. Kamen would lead with founder voice, vertical focus and the proof lane; Matthew holds that the proof lane must be locked before the story goes public. That difference is settled for this brief and carried into the research as a question to test, not a closed one.

## Constraints & guardrails

_Commercial, regulatory, legal, do-not-say, AI and confidential-information limits._

The engagement must not overstate AI capability, certifications, client wins, numbers, speed multipliers or autonomy. The B Team will not claim autonomous AI; it claims governed, checked, reviewable AI — never autonomous, never the product, and always behind the delivered outcome. The company also declines unethical work, and any work that could cause harm to people or exploit them.

## Assets & access

_Research, tracking, past work, data, spokespeople, analytics for baselines._

Available now: the Step 1 desk audits, public review data from Clutch and The Manifest, LinkedIn and directory signals, founder-conversation evidence, Matthew’s public founder voice, and the internal harness proof path. Website analytics is set up, with access through Kamen. Still missing: client-owned sales, referral and talent data, approved client references, named-case permissions, and confirmed measurement baselines — sales pipeline, talent and search tracking do not yet exist and start at zero.

## Success & measurement

_How success is defined; the scorecard sits in the measurement brief._

Success covers buyer trust, proof quality, founder visibility and talent pull in Sofia. The measurement standard is AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the Integrated Evaluation Framework; advertising value equivalents are not used unless the client specifically asks for them. The full scorecard — baseline, target, source, frequency and owner for each measure — is held in the measurement brief, which this brief governs.

## Scope & logistics

_Tier, budget, timeline, markets, decision-maker._

This is a small-and-medium-enterprise brief for a founder-led team. The markets are the United States and the European Union for buyers and Bulgaria for talent. The pilot runs at United Partners' internal cost, and any out-of-pocket costs are decided case by case. No delivery date is fixed beyond the second-quarter-2027 lead objective.

## Decision-maker & approval path

_Who signs, and where a second confirmation is required._

Kamen Kamenov holds final sign-off across the positioning line, proof lane, claims and public references, with no intermediate step. Because Matthew holds the standard that the proof lane must be locked before anything goes public, claim-level and AI-language approvals carry Matthew’s technical confirmation before release, even though Kamen signs. This protects both founders and the agency on exactly the claims most open to challenge.

# Final-brief board -- report

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Two personas, convened on the Step 3 pair before the final-brief hard stop. The CFO asks where the business and the number are behind every measure; the Journalist asks which claim outruns the evidence the material actually supplies. The pair is adjudicated, not advised: a critical finding or a block from either stops the run before approval is even requested.

Convened on the Step 3 pair: The CFO / Board · The Journalist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The CFO / Board | So what — where's the business and the number? | PASS | 0 |
| The Journalist | Where's the substance? I'm going to check. | CONCERN | 1 |

## The findings

### 1. The Journalist — Medium

**Finding.** Success section requires founder visibility and talent pull tracking, but the Measurement Brief scorecard does not include a measure, source, collection frequency or owner for either.

**Quoted target.** "The scorecard sits in the measurement brief and must also track proof quality, founder visibility, search clarity and talent pull."

**Suggested fix.** Add scorecard rows for founder visibility and talent pull, or change the success line to only name dimensions actually measured in Step 3.

## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.

definitions.definition: Artificial intelligence means software techniques that support tasks such as analysis, generation, automation or decision support, without implying autonomous operation.
Governed artificial intelligence means artificial intelligence used with human review, clear checks and visible responsibility for the final work.

research_pack.up_house_style:
## Clear, professional communication language

Every Research document meets the clear, professional communication language standard. The wording is checked sentence by sentence and the whole text is checked end to end, against the rules named in the language standard.

**Wording rules**
- **Plain words:** Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
- **Short sentences:** One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
- **Concrete, not abstract:** Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
- **Proof, not adjectives:** Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
- **Confident, not inflated:** Assured, warm but not casual, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
- **One name per thing:** Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
- **Reader's language, not the method's:** Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's. No process term reaches a client page unexplained.

**Whole-text rules**
- **One clear purpose:** The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
- **Headline first:** Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the story.
- **Logical flow:** Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
- **Right length:** As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
- **Short paragraphs:** One idea per paragraph. If a paragraph runs long, split it. A wall of text goes back.
- **Visual clarity:** Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
- **Self-contained:** A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.

- **Plain words:** Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
- **Short sentences:** One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
- **Concrete, not abstract:** Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
- **Proof, not adjectives:** Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
- **Confident, not inflated:** Assured, warm but not casual, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
- **One name per thing:** Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
- **Reader's language, not the method's:** Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's. No process term reaches a client page unexplained.

**Whole-text rules**
- **One clear purpose:** The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
- **Headline first:** Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the story.
- **Logical flow:** Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
- **Right length:** As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
- **Short paragraphs:** One idea per paragraph. If a paragraph runs long, split it. A wall of text goes back.
- **Visual clarity:** Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
- **Self-contained:** A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.

## Personas — who we are really talking to

Personas are not demographics. These are people, separated by behaviour rather than by age, gender or race.

### Elena

_Elena owns a midsize business and wants better control without becoming technical herself._
