cards.candidate: The B Team can make artificial intelligence (AI) credible only by showing restraint that competitors cannot copy: founder-approved claims, public refusal to overclaim AI, proof assets for each claim and a clear line where the system stops.
cards.insight: For The B Team, the AI story is credible only when restraint is visible. The claim is not that AI makes delivery effortless; it is that senior people govern the work, approve the claim and show where the system stops.
cards.evidence: The approved brief says The B Team claims governed, checked and reviewable AI, never autonomous AI. It also says Kamen Kamenov signs positioning and public references, while Matthew Maday confirms claim-level and AI-language approvals before release. The research pack says The B Team's strongest public proof is trusted software delivery, while public AI proof still needs to be built and approved. The measurement brief defines the proof library as approved assets marked as named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.
cards.tension: The market sells AI as speed and capability. The B Team's safer strategic ground is proof-first restraint: senior-owned delivery, approved claims and a visible stop line before public AI promotion.
cards.so_what: The strategy should not lead with a broad AI promise. It should lead with governed AI behind senior-owned delivery, and no public AI-led claim should ship until the proof library marks the claim as a named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.
cards.audience: Owners of midsize businesses who want more control and visibility without becoming technical buyers themselves.
cards.opportunity: The B Team can own a proof-first restraint position for owners who are interested in AI but do not want vague automation claims. Lexis Solutions, Dreamix, Accedia and Scalefocus can answer with governed delivery language, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder sign-off, approved-reference path, internal proof route and public refusal to overclaim unchanged.
cards.audience_truth: Elena may care more about visibility, ownership and early risk detection than about AI capability. This is a testable audience hypothesis, not settled buyer truth, until owners compare the AI-led message with the control-led message.
cards.ownable_truth: The B Team has proof of trusted software delivery, founder control over claims, approved named-reference routes, a governed AI position and an internal proof path that can show what the system does and where it stops.
cards.how_contrarian: This contradicts the common AI repositioning instinct to sound more capable, faster or more advanced than competitors. It also challenges The B Team to make public restraint part of the offer, not a caveat hidden behind the offer.
cards.what_would_validate_it: Ask owners of midsize businesses to compare two messages: one led by AI development capability and one led by governed control, visible checks, senior ownership and proof limits. The insight is confirmed if owners say the control-led message makes them more willing to take a meeting and feels more credible than the AI-led message. It is refined if they like the control-led message but need named examples, technical proof or sector evidence before they believe it. It is rejected if they prefer the AI-capability message and do not see visibility, ownership or proof limits as a meaningful reason to consider The B Team.

extraction_steps: Immerse — absorb the research pack, the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation read
Generate volume — write many candidates, empirical and intuitive; do not edit yet
So-What ladder — push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated 'so what?'
Screen — test each against the five T's and discard what fails any of them
Find the Sweet Spot — the ownable truth, an insight not yet leveraged, what the audience truly cares about
Distinctiveness Gate — reject anything a competitor could also claim, or the obvious white space everyone sees
Distil — land one to three Killer Insights, no more

# Killer Insight Cards

20 candidates were written and screened; 11 survived; 1 are put forward as cards. Volume first, then judgment.

**Nobody has selected the insight yet.** The volume reserves that for a person: the final insight is chosen, defined and defended by a human, and this engine does not author it on autopilot.

## Card 1

**For The B Team, the AI story is credible only when restraint is visible. The claim is not that AI makes delivery effortless; it is that senior people govern the work, approve the claim and show where the system stops.**

**Type.** intuitive

**The 5 T's.** True: pass — The approved brief says The B Team claims governed, checked and reviewable AI, with founder approval and no autonomous-AI claim. · Tacit: pass — It names restraint as the trust signal beneath the AI repositioning. · Touches the heart: partial — It reassures owners and technical buyers, but the emotional response still needs message testing. · Tension: pass — It sets market AI ambition against proof-first limits. · Triggers action: pass — It directs the strategy to build proof assets, claim approval and a stop line before public AI promotion.

**The tension.** The market sells AI as speed and capability. The B Team's safer strategic ground is proof-first restraint: senior-owned delivery, approved claims and a visible stop line before public AI promotion.

**The audience it is about.** Owners of midsize businesses who want more control and visibility without becoming technical buyers themselves.
**Audience personas.** Elena

**The opportunity it opens.** The B Team can own a proof-first restraint position for owners who are interested in AI but do not want vague automation claims. Lexis Solutions, Dreamix, Accedia and Scalefocus can answer with governed delivery language, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder sign-off, approved-reference path, internal proof route and public refusal to overclaim unchanged.

**What the audience truly cares about.** Elena may care more about visibility, ownership and early risk detection than about AI capability. This is a testable audience hypothesis, not settled buyer truth, until owners compare the AI-led message with the control-led message.

**The company's ownable truth.** The B Team has proof of trusted software delivery, founder control over claims, approved named-reference routes, a governed AI position and an internal proof path that can show what the system does and where it stops.

**Evidence.** The approved brief says The B Team claims governed, checked and reviewable AI, never autonomous AI. It also says Kamen Kamenov signs positioning and public references, while Matthew Maday confirms claim-level and AI-language approvals before release. The research pack says The B Team's strongest public proof is trusted software delivery, while public AI proof still needs to be built and approved. The measurement brief defines the proof library as approved assets marked as named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.

**So what.** The strategy should not lead with a broad AI promise. It should lead with governed AI behind senior-owned delivery, and no public AI-led claim should ship until the proof library marks the claim as a named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.

# The extraction process — seven steps

1. Immerse — absorb the research pack, the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation read
2. Generate volume — write many candidates, empirical and intuitive; do not edit yet
3. So-What ladder — push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated 'so what?'
4. Screen — test each against the five T's and discard what fails any of them
5. Find the Sweet Spot — the ownable truth, an insight not yet leveraged, what the audience truly cares about
6. Distinctiveness Gate — reject anything a competitor could also claim, or the obvious white space everyone sees
7. Distil — land one to three Killer Insights, no more

# Two kinds of insight — and why you need both

| | what it is | proven by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empirical insight | Grounded in data acquired through research methods | The data itself |
| Intuitive insight | Grounded in knowing or sensing, without a rational process | Observation and qualitative evidence — it still needs backup |

**The UP principle.** It is through science that we prove, but through intuition that we discover. The strongest Killer Insights pair an intuitive human truth with empirical proof — the discovery and the evidence together.

# The climb — from data to insight

Insight is a level on a ladder, reached by disciplined questioning — not a lucky thought.

| level | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| Data | Raw, uncontextualised facts ("sales rose 23%") |
| Information | Data organised & compared ("23% — 5 points above target, 8 below history") |
| Insight | What it means, strategically ("the growth is masking a loyalty problem") |
| Foresight | What it signals for the future ("expect margin pressure in 12 months") |

**The tool that climbs it: the So What? test.** For every finding ask "so what?" and keep asking until you reach genuine meaning. Guard against the five traps:

- correlation mistaken for causation
- confirmation bias
- volume mistaken for significance
- the missing counterfactual
- outliers mistaken for trends

# The Sweet Spot

An insight sits where all three meet:

- the company's ownable truth
- an insight not yet leveraged
- what the audience truly cares about

# Step 5B · Validate the insight

A distinctive, contrarian insight cannot lock until it is tested against the real audience. Distinctiveness and wrongness look identical until tested.

## Validating card 1

**How contrarian.** This contradicts the common AI repositioning instinct to sound more capable, faster or more advanced than competitors. It also challenges The B Team to make public restraint part of the offer, not a caveat hidden behind the offer.

**What would validate it.** Ask owners of midsize businesses to compare two messages: one led by AI development capability and one led by governed control, visible checks, senior ownership and proof limits. The insight is confirmed if owners say the control-led message makes them more willing to take a meeting and feels more credible than the AI-led message. It is refined if they like the control-led message but need named examples, technical proof or sector evidence before they believe it. It is rejected if they prefer the AI-capability message and do not see visibility, ownership or proof limits as a meaningful reason to consider The B Team.

**Verdict.** Confirm · Refine · Reject — none recorded. The test has not been run.


# Open — waiting on a person

- **Which of these is the insight?** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.
- **What did the audience say?** — the validation test has not been run, so no verdict is recorded.

# Insight mini-board — report

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Three personas, convened at step 5B against the insight alone, to kill a weak insight before a whole strategy is built on it. The Competitor asks whether they could claim it word for word, the Target Audience whether they recognise themselves in it, the Activist what it looks like turned over. It is not the pre-ship board and it does not clear the work; it stops one thing from being built on.

Convened at step 5B: The Competitor · The Target Audience · The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Competitor | I can say that too. | PASS | 0 |
| The Target Audience | Why do I care? I don't believe you. | PASS | 0 |
| The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist | Here's how this blows up. | CONCERN | 2 |

## The findings

### 1. The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist — Medium

**Finding.** The competitor contrast creates an avoidable counter-attack because named peers could challenge the claim that they cannot match the restraint position.

**Quoted target.** "Lexis Solutions, Dreamix, Accedia and Scalefocus can answer with governed delivery language, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder sign-off, approved-reference path, internal proof route and public refusal to overclaim unchanged."

**Suggested fix.** Keep the insight, but rewrite the peer contrast as an internal ownability claim until competitor proof has been checked line by line: The B Team can make restraint ownable through founder sign-off, approved references, internal proof and refusal to overclaim.

### 2. The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist — Medium

**Finding.** The insight names public refusal to overclaim as a differentiator, which can become a target if critics ask for examples of refused claims or harmful work boundaries.

**Quoted target.** "public refusal to overclaim AI"

**Suggested fix.** Before building the strategy on this, define the refusal boundary in practical terms: what The B Team will not claim, what work it declines, who approves exceptions, and what proof is publishable.

## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.

# Strategy One-Pager

The one page everything else flows from. A gap here is a gap in the thinking.

**The approach is decided:** The Stop Line, recorded by Kamen Kamenov. The options below show the evaluation it was chosen from.

Engagement tier: standard-enterprise — the ten boxes of this page are the complete set for this tier.

Claim boundary: Kamen Kamenov gives final sign-off on positioning, proof lane, claims and public references. Matthew Maday gives technical confirmation for claim-level and AI-language approvals before release.

Concept boundary: The fixed concept is proof-first restraint: The B Team makes AI credible by showing evidence, senior responsibility and limits. In public, it should be shown through approved proof, demonstrations, references and stop lines, not proclaimed as a superiority claim.

## Executive summary (2–3 lines)

The strategy should make restraint visible before The B Team promotes its artificial intelligence (AI) story.

It speaks first to Elena, the owner who wants more control and visibility without becoming technical.

The public story should show approved proof, senior responsibility and clear limits before it asks buyers to believe the AI claim.

## Business & communication objectives (SMART+I)

Refreshed at the annual review for the coming year — re-approval pending in writing.

By 30 June 2027, increase recognition of The B Team as the proof-led AI engineering partner behind The Stop Line among owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers from the baseline set in the first message-testing wave before launch to the target set in that same wave, contributing to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union.

By 30 June 2027, increase trust in The Stop Line among CTOs and architecture owners from the baseline set in the first buyer interview or survey wave before launch to the target set in that same wave, contributing to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union.

By 30 June 2027, increase understanding of Signed by Humans among owners of midsize businesses from the baseline set in the first owner message test before launch to the target set in that same test, contributing to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union.

By 30 June 2027, decrease unresolved public-profile conflicts among buyer-facing public records from six unresolved conflict areas to zero, contributing to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union.

By 30 June 2027, increase qualified enterprise leads connected to The Stop Line among buyers in the United States and the European Union from sales tracking starting at zero on 25 August 2026 to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter, contributing to the same enterprise-lead objective.

## Target audience profile & persona

Target audience profile & persona: The strategy leads with owners of midsize businesses who want control and visibility, then equips technical buyers, including chief technology officers and architecture owners, with proof. It also supports senior Sofia talent with a craft-led AI story. Persona: Elena.

## The strategic approach + one-line positioning

Approach: Proof-first restraint.

Positioning: The B Team makes AI credible by showing the proof, the people responsible and the line it will not cross.

Positioning (lead line): Restraint is the proof.

**Positioning (lead line).** Restraint is the proof.

**Expression options for the person to choose from.** The concept is fixed; the public expression is open. Candidates: “Proof before promise” (restraint before promotion), “Where AI stops, trust starts” (visible limits as trust), “Senior-owned AI delivery” (human responsibility behind AI). The choice belongs to a person and is tested with the audience before public use.

**It holds only if.** The recommended approach is believable only if the proof library, public identity cleanup and claim approval route are visible before public AI promotion. Buyers must be able to see what is proved, who owns the claim and where AI stops. If that condition fails, restraint stops looking like discipline and starts looking like a claim without proof.

## Core narrative & 3–5 key messages

Core narrative: The B Team is not asking buyers to trust AI because it sounds fast or advanced. It asks them to trust AI-supported delivery only where senior people govern the work, approve the claim and show where the system stops.

Key messages: AI supports the work; senior people still own the outcome. Every public AI claim must connect to approved proof. The B Team will not claim autonomous AI. The proof comes before the promotion. Clear limits make the AI story easier to trust.

## Proof points / supporting evidence

The approved brief says The B Team claims governed, checked and reviewable AI, never autonomous AI. The approved brief says Kamen Kamenov signs positioning, proof lane, claims and public references. The approved brief says Matthew Maday confirms claim-level and AI-language approvals before release. The research pack says The B Team's strongest public proof is trusted software delivery, while public AI proof still needs to be built and approved. The measurement brief says proof assets must be marked as named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.

## Channel strategy (PESO)

Paid, Earned, Shared and Owned (PESO) shape: earned activity leads once the proof library and public identity cleanup are ready, because the reputation gap needs independent credibility. Owned proof pages and founder-led shared posts prepare the evidence; paid activity supports targeted testing and retargeting only.

**Why this leads.** Earned media leads because the gap is credibility, not reach. Owned and shared channels can state the proof, but independent validation makes the repositioning harder to dismiss.

## Campaign timeline & phases

No delivery date is established beyond 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027). The practical order is public identity cleanup, proof library lock, message testing, founder-led proof launch and earned validation.

**The phasing spine.** 1) Clean the public identity. 2) Lock the proof library. 3) Test the control-led message. 4) Launch founder-led proof. 5) Earn third-party validation.

## Success metrics & KPIs

Measurement follows the Association for Measurement and Evaluation of Communication Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the Integrated Evaluation Framework. Core measures are proof credibility, technical-buyer trust, public-profile consistency, founder visibility and talent pull in Sofia.

## Budget allocation summary · risk mitigation

The pilot runs at United Partners' internal cost, and out-of-pocket costs are decided case by case. The main risks are an AI story that outruns proof, public identity inconsistency, unapproved references and unclear data or AI claims.

**Issues preparedness.** Under public or buyer challenge, the approach holds because it carries fewer claims and each claim has an approval route and proof type. If evidence is missing, the message narrows instead of defending a broad AI promise.

# The Strategy Blueprint cascade

Everything in line of sight: business objective → communication objective → strategic approach → narrative → messages → pillars → platform → tactics → KPIs.

**Business objective.** Win two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union by 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027).

**Communication objective (SMART+I).** By 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027), make owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers see The B Team as a proof-led artificial intelligence (AI) engineering partner by publishing only approved, traceable AI claims and lifting buyer trust, proof credibility and founder visibility above their first recorded baselines.

**How it traces.** The communication objective serves the business objective by giving qualified buyers a clear, proved reason to trust the AI story and take a meeting before the lead target date.

# The decision rule

If a message cannot show the approved proof behind the AI claim, the senior owner responsible for it and the line the system will not cross, it does not ship.

The team's day-to-day test for whether a message belongs.

# The options it was chosen from

Weak strategy is the first plausible approach written up confidently. These are the alternatives and how each scored.

## Option 1 — Proof-first restraint

**Shape.** Own the tension

**Direction.** GET owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers and senior Sofia talent WHO see AI claims as easy to overstate TO see The B Team as the AI engineering partner that proves what it claims BY making every public claim traceable to approved proof, senior ownership and visible limits.

**Positioning.** The B Team makes AI credible by showing the proof, the people responsible and the line it will not cross.

| Fit | It resolves the insight's tension because it turns restraint into the trust signal that can move buyers toward a meeting. |
| Distinctiveness | Competitors can claim governance, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder sign-off, approved-reference route and refusal to overclaim unchanged. |
| Feasibility | The client can do it if the proof library, public identity cleanup and claim approval route are visible before public release. |
| Durability | It can survive a year and a bad news cycle because fewer, approved and traceable claims are easier to defend than broad AI promises. |

## Option 2 — Visible owner control

**Shape.** Close the trust gap **Direction.** GET owners of midsize businesses WHO want AI benefits but fear losing control TO see The B Team as the partner that makes work, risk and delivery visible BY translating governed AI into plain control, review and accountability signals. **Positioning.** The B Team gives owners clearer control over AI-supported delivery. **Rejected —** It speaks well to Elena, but it does not carry enough technical proof on its own.

## Option 3 — Architect-led AI engineering

**Shape.** Reposition **Direction.** GET technical buyers WHO doubt newer AI claims from a small software firm TO accept The B Team as a serious AI engineering partner BY leading with architecture ownership, review discipline, technical artifacts and approved delivery proof. **Positioning.** The B Team brings senior architecture discipline to governed AI delivery. **Rejected —** It can satisfy technical buyers, but it narrows the story before the owner-control opportunity is tested.

# UP's recommendation

**Recommended.** Proof-first restraint

It is strongest across fit, distinctiveness, feasibility and durability because it answers the core tension with a proof route The B Team can actually operate. It also gives the other two routes a role without letting either narrow the strategy too early.

**Coverage.** The B Team serves owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers and senior Sofia talent. This approach covers all three with one idea: AI is credible when proof, senior ownership and limits are visible.

**Why not the others.** Visible owner control — It speaks well to Elena, but it does not carry enough technical proof on its own. Architect-led AI engineering — It can satisfy technical buyers, but it narrows the story before the owner-control opportunity is tested.

The recommendation is United Partners'; the recorded decision below confirms it.

# Open — waiting on a person

- **Which approach do we take?** — decided: The Stop Line (recorded by Kamen Kamenov).
- **Which public expression?** — “Proof before promise”, “Where AI stops, trust starts”, “Senior-owned AI delivery” — tested with the audience before public use; no owner recorded.

# The Creative Big Idea

Built through the IdeaHaus method — creativity with structure. A Big Idea is the single organising thought that makes an audience feel something and act, and that a whole programme of work can hang from for years. It is the elevated purpose; a tactic is the activity that serves it. The most common creative failure is presenting the second dressed as the first.

12 candidates were generated and 2 were marked as tactics rather than ideas. 3 are built out below.

**Decided.** Recorded at the foot of this document as a nested platform and launch expression — Kamen Kamenov.

## The elevated objective

**What the client asked for.** The B Team needs a campaign idea that makes its artificial intelligence story credible to owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers without overstating what AI can do.

**The value we add.** United Partners turns restraint from a safety caveat into a public trust signal: proof, senior responsibility and a visible line that AI does not cross.

**Elevated (NEED + VALUE = POWER).** Make The B Team the company that changes how ambitious businesses judge AI partners: not by who promises the most automation, but by who can show the proof, the people responsible and the line where the system stops.

**Result-back (the movie ending).** On launch day, owners, technical buyers and peers are pointing to The B Team's line in the sand and asking their own partners where AI stops and human responsibility begins. The campaign has succeeded when the market repeats the demand: show me the proof, show me the person and show me the stop line.

## The insights

**AI becomes more credible for The B Team when restraint is visible, because the buyer's real fear is not weak technology; it is losing control of responsibility, evidence and judgement.** (intuitive) — This follows from the approved brief's proof-first restraint position and the audience hypothesis that owners value control and visibility without becoming technical buyers.

| T | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| True | Pass: it fits the approved strategy and the stated audience concern. |
| Tacit | Pass: it names restraint as the hidden trust signal beneath AI interest. |
| Touches the heart | Partial: it reassures anxious owners, but the emotional pull still needs audience testing. |
| Tension | Pass: it sets market AI ambition against the need for limits. |
| Triggers action | Pass: it points directly to proof assets, claim approval and visible stop lines. |

**A smaller AI claim can feel stronger than a larger one when the proof is cleaner, the owner is visible and the limit is explicit.** (empirical) — The research pack says The B Team's strongest public proof is trusted software delivery, while public AI proof still needs to be built and approved.

| T | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| True | Pass: the evidence supports a narrower public claim route. |
| Tacit | Pass: it reveals why restraint can feel like confidence. |
| Touches the heart | Partial: it builds trust, but it may need a sharper human story to move beyond reassurance. |
| Tension | Pass: it challenges the category instinct to sound bigger. |
| Triggers action | Pass: it directs the launch to fewer claims and better evidence. |

## The three built out

A true Big Idea is also: about the brand's purpose/benefit; stands out in its category; radically opens hearts and minds; creates movement.

### The Stop Line

**In one sentence.** The B Team makes AI credible by publicly showing the point where automation stops and senior human responsibility takes over.

**The elevated purpose.** Change the buyer's question from 'what can your AI do?' to 'where does your AI stop, and who is responsible after that?'

**Why it works.** It turns the client's proof-first restraint into a memorable market demand that competitors can discuss but cannot copy with the same founder sign-off, approved claim route and refusal to overclaim.

**The movement it creates.** Owners ask for a stop line before they trust an AI partner; technical buyers test claims against proof; institutions and peers borrow the language to demand clearer limits.

**Why it meets the IdeaHaus bar.** It meets the IdeaHaus bar because it is about The B Team's benefit, stands out from inflated AI promises, opens hearts through reassurance and creates movement by giving buyers a question to ask.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Simple | Pass: the idea is easy to repeat because it turns trust into one concrete image, a line that AI does not cross. |
| Shareable | Pass: 'show me the stop line' gives buyers, founders and technical leaders a phrase they can use in posts, sales conversations and scrutiny. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can stretch from a website line to proof pages, demos, events, sales tools and earned media. |
| Memorable | Pass: the phrase is visual and contrasts sharply with the category's usual speed and capability language. |
| Ownable | Pass: competitors can claim governance, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder approval route, proof library and public refusal to overclaim unchanged. |
| Persuasive | Pass with a condition: it persuades only if every public claim links to approved proof and a named human approval route. |

### Signed by Humans

**In one sentence.** Every AI claim from The B Team carries visible human ownership before it reaches the market.

**The elevated purpose.** Make human responsibility the proof mark that separates serious AI delivery from loose automation talk.

**Why it works.** It makes the abstract promise of governance feel personal, accountable and repeatable by showing that a senior person approves the claim before the market sees it.

**The movement it creates.** Buyers start asking who signed the claim; teams attach human approval to AI work; public proof shifts from system capability to accountable responsibility.

**Why it meets the IdeaHaus bar.** It meets the IdeaHaus bar because it carries the brand benefit, opens hearts through accountability and creates a visible behavior people can copy or demand.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Simple | Pass: the idea is clear in three words and needs little explanation. |
| Shareable | Pass: it works as a public prompt, proof mark and launch expression. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can appear on claim pages, case studies, technical artifacts, demos and leadership posts. |
| Memorable | Pass: it gives the campaign a human signature in a category full of machine language. |
| Ownable | Partial: the phrase is strong for The B Team, but another firm could imitate the signature device unless The B Team ties it tightly to its approval route and proof library. |
| Persuasive | Pass: it makes accountability visible and lowers the risk of vague AI claims. |

### Fewer Promises, Better Proof

**In one sentence.** The B Team earns trust by making fewer AI claims and proving each one more clearly.

**The elevated purpose.** Make restraint feel like confidence: a company that can prove its claims does not need to inflate them.

**Why it works.** It attacks the category habit of sounding bigger and gives The B Team a disciplined way to launch before its public AI proof is fully mature.

**The movement it creates.** Buyers reward evidence over volume; sales conversations narrow to what can be proved; the company cuts any claim that has no approved proof type.

**Why it meets the IdeaHaus bar.** It meets part of the IdeaHaus bar because it supports the brand benefit and stands apart from overclaiming, but it is more strategic discipline than full emotional platform.

| criterion | judgement |

| Scalable | Pass: it can guide messaging, proof assets, media interviews and sales enablement. |
| Memorable | The thought is strong, but the wording is harder to make yours and less easy to picture than the platform wording already approved for use. |
| Ownable | Weak: disciplined proof is credible for The B Team, but many competitors could claim a similar stance. |
| Persuasive | Pass: it turns the client's limited public AI proof into a disciplined trust position. |

## The volume it came from

Creativity without structure is chaos. Every candidate below names the trainer that produced it, and whether it is really an idea or a tactic — the mayonnaise-versus-sandwich test.

| candidate | trainer | idea or tactic |

| The Stop Line | Challenge Idea | idea |
| Signed by Humans | Movement | idea |
| Where AI Stops, Trust Starts | Provocation | idea |
| The Receipts Before the Robot | Random Entry | idea |
| No Claim Leaves Alone | Movement | idea |
| The Human Approval Layer | Provocation | tactic |
| Fewer Promises, Better Proof | Challenge Idea | idea |
| The Line We Will Not Cross | Provocation | idea |
| Proof Has a Signature | Random Entry | idea |
| Show the Stop | Challenge Idea | tactic |
| AI With an Adult in the Room | Provocation | idea |
| Every Claim Has an Owner | Movement | idea |

## The six IdeaHaus steps, as applied

1. Internalize the strategy — The work starts from proof-first restraint, with AI made credible through approved proof, senior responsibility and visible limits.
2. Result-back thinking — The campaign ending is a market behavior: buyers ask every AI partner to show the proof, the person responsible and the stop line.
3. Embrace insights — The WHO truths are that owners may value control and visibility more than AI capability language (intuitive), and the approved brief supports governed, checked and reviewable AI rather than autonomous AI (empirical).
4. Elevate the objectives — The objective moves from promoting The B Team's AI story to changing how buyers judge responsible AI partners.
5. Focused ideation — The four trainers produced headlines that forced restraint, signatures, proof and limits into campaign-scale ideas rather than claim checks alone.
6. Validate against the Big Idea Criteria — The built ideas were tested for simplicity, shareability, scale, memory, ownership, persuasion and their ability to create real buyer movement.

## Validation against the IdeaHaus Big Idea Criteria

The eight criteria, applied to the recommended direction. Where a criterion is only partly met, it is marked so — the check must discriminate.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| About the brand's purpose/benefit | Pass: The Stop Line expresses The B Team's benefit as governed AI delivery with senior responsibility and proof. |
| Stands out in its category | Pass: it rejects the category's usual speed and capability race and makes visible restraint the trust signal. |
| Radically opens heart & mind | Pass with a condition: it can change how buyers feel about AI risk, but only if the proof feels human and not procedural. |
| Simple | Pass: the idea is short, visual and easy to repeat. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can scale across positioning, website, proof library, demos, sales tools, founder content and earned media. |
| Recognisable, memorable asset | Pass: the stop line is a repeatable verbal and visual asset. |
| Creates movement | Pass: it gives buyers a concrete demand: show me where AI stops and who takes responsibility. |
| Shareable, any-size screen | Partial: the phrase travels well, but the proof detail behind it must be simplified for small-screen use. |

**The claim guardrail still holds.** The idea can be big, but every claim stays small enough to prove. Public AI language must remain governed, checked and reviewable, with each claim tied to approved proof, a responsible human and a clear line the system does not cross; the bigger the platform becomes, the more important that proof discipline becomes.

## Two conditions carried into execution

1 · **Proof before public scale.** No public AI claim ships unless it is approved and tied to one proof type: named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.

2 · **Human ceiling for emotional altitude.** A named human owner must protect the emotional height of The Stop Line and Signed by Humans when they become pages, posts, demos and sales tools, so the work does not collapse into proof mechanics alone.


## The Big Idea — decided

**Platform:** The Stop Line.

**Launch expression:** Signed by Humans.

**Why nested rather than chosen.** The Stop Line is the bigger, category-shaping idea but it needs a concrete proof mechanism to be believed; Signed by Humans is that mechanism — a named person stands behind every claim — and it needs the larger idea to belong to. The platform sets the standard; the launch expression proves it person by person.

**How it runs.** Signed by Humans launches the idea and makes it tangible on the website, founder content and buyer meetings — every public claim carries the name of the person who proved it; The Stop Line carries the category conversation above it and holds the next expression after the signed campaign has run.

**Owner of the decision.** Recorded as the human strategist call (Kamen Kamenov), taken from the three built-out candidates. The engine generated the volume; the nesting and the choice are the strategist's.

# Message Architecture

One connected architecture, not three separate lists. Every message and every pillar traces back to the one story; anything that does not, does not belong.

**Waiting on an owner.** The story's truth and its tension belong to a person, and no owner has approved them in writing yet.

## Rebuilt from the Big Idea

This architecture is built from the Big Idea the strategist decided — The Stop Line, launched through Signed by Humans — not from the nearest provable frame. The idea's role is the spine; the first-believer audience is the first proof of it, not the whole story.

## The narrative

**World.** Artificial intelligence (AI) has made software claims easier to make and harder to trust. Owners want the benefit, but they need to see who is responsible, what is proved and where the system stops.

**Tension.** The market pulls AI stories toward speed and capability. The B Team's credible ground pulls the other way: fewer claims, approved proof, senior responsibility and visible limits.

**Resolution.** The tension resolves when restraint becomes the trust signal. The B Team leads with The Stop Line, so every AI claim shows the proof behind it, the people responsible for it and the limit it will not cross.

**Our role.** The B Team's role is to make governed AI believable by making the stop line public, provable and Signed by Humans.

### In the UP template

**We believe in a world where…** AI-supported delivery should be useful without becoming vague, hidden or unowned.

**We know…** Buyers do not need a bigger AI promise. They need proof they can inspect, senior people they can hold accountable and a clear line the system will not cross.

**So we make sure…** Every public AI claim is approved, traceable and limited to what The B Team can prove.

**Which is why we…** Work from The Stop Line: proof first, senior ownership visible and every claim Signed by Humans.

### Compressed

**Trailer.** Elena wants the control and visibility AI can bring, but she does not want to become technical to know whether the work is safe. The B Team has to show her where AI helps, where people stay responsible and where the system stops.

**Tweet.** The B Team makes AI credible by showing The Stop Line: approved proof, senior ownership and the clear limit the system will not cross. Every claim is traceable. Every serious promise is Signed by Humans.

## Key messages

The six-type Messaging Architecture — Awareness, Relevance, Emotion, Logic, Action, Commitment — under one umbrella message. Each message laddered with the Trident: 1° umbrella claim → 2° supporting pillar → 3° killer fact.

cd_s_002.communications_platform_markdown:
# The Communications Platform

An architecture, not a list. If the channels could each belong to a different strategy, this would be a list.

**No platform has been chosen.** The candidates and their tests are below; the choice, and the judgement of what is genuinely ownable, belong to a person.

## Candidate platforms, against the five criteria

### Candidate 1 — The Stop Line

**Why it is ownable.** The B Team can own this platform if it makes restraint visible through approved proof, named senior responsibility and clear limits before any artificial intelligence claim reaches the market.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Differentiation | It differentiates The B Team by refusing the broad artificial intelligence promise and showing the proof, owner and limit behind each claim. |
| Heritage | It fits The B Team's strongest established proof: trusted software delivery, senior judgment and careful claims. |
| Extension | It can extend into proof pages, founder posts, partner packs, technical artifacts, sales material and talent content without changing the idea. |
| Competitive advantage | Competitors can talk about governance, but they cannot copy The B Team's approval route, named senior ownership and approved proof library unchanged. |
| Durable / global | It can travel across the United States, the European Union and Sofia because trust, proof and human responsibility are not local claims. |

### Candidate 2 — Signed by Humans

**Why it is ownable.** The B Team can own this platform if every serious artificial intelligence claim carries a visible human signature: who checked it, what proof supports it and where the system stops.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Differentiation | It stands apart because it makes human responsibility the proof point, not a decorative reassurance after an artificial intelligence claim. |
| Heritage | It draws from The B Team's senior craft and approval discipline, which are already central to the strategy. |
| Extension | It can support founder visibility, technical credibility, recruitment, partner enablement and buyer follow-up because each use shows human ownership. |
| Competitive advantage | It creates a practical trust mechanism competitors cannot easily copy unless they expose their own approval route and senior accountability. |
| Durable / global | It is durable because buyers in different markets can understand a simple promise: a senior person still owns the work. |

## PESO, orchestrated around one insight

PESO (Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned) is the channel architecture the platform orchestrates against. Earned-led, because for corporate reputation third-party credibility is what builds trust.

| channel | its role here | the volume's role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paid | Paid supports targeted message testing, retargeting and amplification after proof exists; it drives buyers and partners to owned proof pages, then lifts earned stories and shared founder content rather than carrying the reputation story alone. | Controlled reach and action — support, selective |
| Earned | Earned leads this corporate reputation platform once the proof library and public identity cleanup are ready, because independent validation makes The Stop Line harder to dismiss and gives paid, shared and owned channels stronger proof to carry. | Third-party credibility and validation — the reputation engine, and it leads |
| Shared | Shared makes senior ownership visible through founder, executive and team posts; it points audiences to owned proof, gives influencers and partners material they can repeat and helps paid amplification reach warmer audiences. | Participation and advocacy — support |
| Owned | Owned is the proof base: website pages, proof library, approval language, case material, technical artifacts and sales follow-ups; paid drives to it, earned cites it and shared content turns it into a steady public signal. | Depth, education and conversion — the foundation |

## The 4C integrated programming model

Unifying Human Insight → Find the Right Moment → Deploy the Right Channels → Engage Influencers → Develop Compelling Content → Evaluate & Recalibrate.

## The engagement model

How an audience is moved, stage by stage. The stages are not interchangeable: nobody is mobilised who was never engaged, and advocacy asked for before connection is noise.

| stage | what it is for |
| --- | --- |
| Align / Engage | reach the audience where they already are, on something they already care about |
| Develop / Enhance | deepen what they understand, so the relationship survives one message |
| Connect / Advocate | give them a reason and a means to say it themselves |
| Mobilise / Amplify | turn that into visible action at a scale that changes the picture |

**Underneath all four, always on.** Campaigns punctuate this baseline; they are not the baseline. A plan of bursts with nothing underneath cannot hold a reputation between them.

- **Conversation Management loop.** listen, triage, respond and escalate on what is already being said, every day, whether or not a campaign is running
- **The Observatory newsroom.** watch the environment for the moments worth entering, and be ready to publish into them before they close

## Activation Cards

No tactic goes on the calendar until it is a card, and every card traces up to an audience, a message and a pillar.

### Card 1 — The Stop Line proof page

**Insight.** Buyers do not need a bigger artificial intelligence promise; they need to see what is proved, who owns it and where the system stops.

**Idea.** Create one owned page that introduces The Stop Line and shows each approved claim with its proof type, senior owner and stated limit.

**Engagement.** Visitors can inspect the proof behind the claim before they are asked to book a meeting or accept the artificial intelligence story.

**Outcome.** The B Team has a public proof base that paid, earned, shared and sales activity can all point to.

**Line of sight.** Owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers, partners and senior Sofia talent. · The B Team makes artificial intelligence credible by showing The Stop Line before it promotes the claim. · The Stop Line makes restraint visible.

**Channel.** Owned  ·  **KPI (key performance indicator).** Proof-page visits, time on page, qualified meeting clicks and percentage of public artificial intelligence claims linked to approved proof.  ·  **Phase.** Proof library lock and founder-led proof launch.

### Card 2 — Signed by Humans founder launch post

**Insight.** The human moment makes the artificial intelligence story credible when a senior person visibly checks, owns and signs the work.

**Idea.** Publish a founder-led launch post that explains Signed by Humans as the visible promise behind The Stop Line.

**Engagement.** Readers see the senior responsibility behind the claim and are directed to the owned proof page for evidence.

**Outcome.** Founder visibility increases while the public story stays inside the approved proof boundary.

**Line of sight.** Owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers, referral partners and senior Sofia talent. · Signed by Humans means senior people still own the outcome. · Signed by Humans means senior people own the outcome.

**Channel.** Shared  ·  **KPI.** Founder-post reach, engagement quality, proof-page clicks, partner reshares and qualified inbound conversations.  ·  **Phase.** Founder-led proof launch.

### Card 3 — Partner proof pack

**Insight.** Referral partners can carry the story only if the approved proof is simple, repeatable and safe to share.

**Idea.** Build a short partner pack that explains The Stop Line, Signed by Humans and the approved proof types behind each claim.

**Engagement.** Partners get language they can use without inventing claims or stretching evidence.

**Outcome.** Referral conversations become easier, more consistent and less exposed to unapproved artificial intelligence claims.

**Line of sight.** Referral partners, ecosystem partners and enterprise buyers. · Every artificial intelligence claim earns its place through approved proof before it reaches the market. · Proof comes before promotion.

**Channel.** Owned and Earned  ·  **KPI.** Partner pack downloads, partner briefings completed, referred qualified leads and claim-compliance checks.  ·  **Phase.** Earn third-party validation.

### Card 4 — Owner control message test

**Insight.** Elena's preference for control and visibility is a strong hypothesis, but it is not settled buyer truth until owners compare the messages.

**Idea.** Test a control-led message against an artificial-intelligence-capability message, both anchored in The Stop Line.

**Engagement.** Owners react to plain-language options that show visibility, ownership and early risk detection without asking them to become technical buyers.

**Outcome.** The B Team learns whether control should lead owner-facing communication before scaling the message.

**Line of sight.** Owners of midsize businesses, led by Elena. · Owners get more control and visibility without having to become technical buyers themselves. · Owners get control without becoming technical.

**Channel.** Paid and Owned  ·  **KPI.** Preference split, comprehension score, trust lift, meeting intent and qualitative reasons for choice.  ·  **Phase.** Message testing.

### Card 5 — Senior craft story series

**Insight.** Senior Sofia talent and careful buyers will believe the artificial intelligence story only if it protects judgment rather than celebrating automation alone.

**Idea.** Publish a recurring series under Signed by Humans that shows how senior people review work, make decisions and define the stop line.

**Engagement.** Readers see craft, judgment and responsibility inside artificial intelligence-supported delivery.

**Outcome.** The talent story and buyer story reinforce each other without turning The B Team into a broad ethics platform.

**Line of sight.** Senior Sofia talent and buyers who want craft behind artificial intelligence-supported delivery. · The human moment is the hand on the work: someone senior checks it, owns it and signs it before it is put in front of a buyer. · Senior craft keeps judgment in the work.

**Channel.** Shared and Owned  ·  **KPI.** Senior-talent engagement, profile visits, qualified candidate interest, buyer engagement and proof-page clicks.  ·  **Phase.** Always-on after launch.

## The Communications Plan

### The platform idea and why it is ownable

The platform is The Stop Line, launched through Signed by Humans. Its purpose is to make The B Team's artificial intelligence story credible by showing approved proof, senior responsibility and the limit the system will not cross before any claim is promoted.

### Rollout strategies and phasing

The rollout should move in this order: clean the public identity, lock the proof library, test the control-led owner message, launch the founder-led proof story and then seek earned validation. No delivery date is established beyond 30 June 2027.

### Target audiences prioritised, each with its channels and tactics

The plan leads with owners of midsize businesses who want control and visibility, then equips technical buyers with proof. It also supports referral partners, ecosystem partners, enterprise buyers and senior Sofia talent with the same story, adapted to their role.

### The PESO channel architecture, earned-led and integrated

Owned runs always-on as the proof base: proof pages, approval language, case material, technical artifacts, sales follow-ups and frequently asked questions. Shared runs always-on through founder, executive and team posts. The newsroom watches for artificial intelligence trust, governance and buyer-risk moments, then responds only when The B Team has approved proof and a clear stop line to show. Earned leads reputation once proof exists, while paid supports testing, retargeting and amplification.

### The tactics as Activation Cards

The main tactics are The Stop Line proof page, Signed by Humans founder launch post, partner proof pack, owner control message test and senior craft story series. Each tactic must trace to an audience, a key message and a communications pillar before it goes on the calendar.

### The 12-month content calendar

The calendar should not be built as campaign bursts only. It should combine a few hero moments with steady hub content and hygiene updates, with the middle carrying most of the programme through proof pages, founder posts, buyer explainers, partner material and technical artifacts.

### The integrated plan and messages, sequenced

The sequence is proof before promotion. If a claim cannot show approved proof, a senior owner and the line the system will not cross, it does not ship; where approval or evidence is not established, the plan must say so instead of filling the gap.

## The Pyramid of Influence

The voices who carry the story, from the top down.

| level | who they are |
| --- | --- |
| Professional Influencers | journalists, analysts, named experts |
| The Power Middle | semi-pro creators, sector voices |
| Super Fans & Employees | the people who already carry it without being asked |
| Fans & Followers | the audience that amplifies what it already believes |

For corporate reputation the highest-value influencers are usually credible third parties — analysts, editors, respected alumni or partners — and employees as advocates.

## The pull-through line of sight

Vision / Position → Brand Expression → Go-to-Market → Communications Programs.

## Open — waiting on a person

- **Which platform do we build?** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.

# Execution Toolkit

The bridge from an approved strategy to activity on the ground: a self-contained pack any team, market or partner can run to the same standard, without the strategist in the room.

**4 of 10 assets still to be produced.** They are listed as such rather than implied to exist.

**Not approved.** The assets and the do-not-say lines are a person's to approve, and no owner has.

## A · The strategic foundation

**Platform recap.** The platform is The Stop Line, launched through Signed by Humans. It makes The B Team's artificial intelligence (AI) story credible by showing approved proof, senior responsibility and the limit the system will not cross before any AI claim reaches the market.

**Story skeleton.** Insight: AI has made software claims easier to make and harder to trust. Owners want the benefit, but they need to see who is responsible, what is proved and where the system stops. · Reason to Believe: The B Team's approved brief claims governed, checked and reviewable AI, not autonomous AI. The claim boundary names Kamen Kamenov as final sign-off for positioning, proof lane, claims and public references, and Matthew Maday as technical confirmation for claim-level and AI-language approvals before release. · Benefit: Buyers, partners and senior talent can understand the AI story without accepting a broad promise on trust alone. · Proof: The proof library must mark each approved asset as a named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo. Each public AI claim must show its proof type, senior owner and stated limit.

**Strategy recap.** The rollout follows proof before promotion. The programme cleans public identity, locks the proof library, tests the owner control message, launches the founder-led proof story and then seeks earned validation. Owned proof is the foundation, earned media leads reputation after proof exists, shared content makes senior ownership visible and paid media supports testing, retargeting and amplification.

## B · The plan

### Pre-Seed / Tease

**Objective.** Prepare the proof base before the market sees the AI story.

**Audience.** Owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers, referral partners, ecosystem partners, enterprise buyers and senior Sofia talent.

**Messages.** The Stop Line makes AI easier to trust because it shows what is proved, who owns it and where the system stops.

**Activities.** Clean public identity, lock approved proof, prepare the Key-Message Table, build the proof page, prepare the Q&A (questions and answers) / FAQ (frequently asked questions) and brief spokespeople.

### Launch

**Objective.** Introduce The Stop Line through Signed by Humans and direct audiences to approved proof.

**Audience.** Owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers, partners and senior Sofia talent.

**Messages.** The B Team makes AI credible by showing The Stop Line before it promotes the AI claim. Every serious promise is Signed by Humans.

**Activities.** Publish the proof page, issue the founder launch post, release the press release, run the 30-second pitch, publish the fact sheet and activate the social pack.

### Sustain

**Objective.** Keep the platform visible between launch moments through proof, explanation and senior ownership.

**Audience.** Owners, technical buyers, partners and senior Sofia talent.

**Messages.** Owners get control without becoming technical. Signed by Humans means senior people still own the outcome. Proof comes before promotion.

**Activities.** Run the owner message test, publish buyer explainers, continue senior craft stories, share approved technical artifacts and keep the Conversation Management loop active.

### Amplify

**Objective.** Use proof and third-party credibility to extend the story without widening the claim.

**Audience.** Referral partners, ecosystem partners, enterprise buyers, professional influencers, employees and followers.

**Messages.** Every AI claim earns its place through approved proof before it reaches the market.

**Activities.** Brief partners, pitch earned validation after proof exists, equip employees, amplify the strongest proof-led content and recalibrate from campaign measurement.

## D · Activation & execution

- Influencer and creator activation, including disclosure

## The build workflow — assembling the toolkit

| step | what you do | output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Recap the platform | Distil the approved strategy to a one-page foundation the toolkit can stand on | Platform + story skeleton |
| 2 Phase the plan | Break the roadmap into Pre-Seed → Launch → Sustain → Amplify with objectives per phase | Phased plan |
| 3 Build the calendar | Lay the messages and moments onto a month-by-month calendar per audience track | Editorial calendar |
| 4 Write the message tracks | Turn key messages into audience-ready copy, incl. what they'll say and see | Message tracks |
| 5 Produce the collateral | Create the ready-to-use assets from templates | Collateral library |
| 6 Write the guidelines | Channel, influencer, localisation, logistics, measurement, governance | Activation guidelines |
| 7 Package & QA (quality assurance) | Assemble; run the pre-publish quality gate; version and distribute | The toolkit |

## Influencer and creator activation

A repeatable way to activate creators, with the targets stated up front rather than negotiated each time.

**Targets, per creator.** 1 blog / long post · 3–5 social updates over ~14 days · 2–3 posts per day during a live challenge · an agreed number of pieces committed up front

**Golden rules.** be relevant & targeted · crowd-source their expertise · personalise — never cut-and-paste · make it easy — ready assets, local adaptation · be transparent and require disclosure of gifted product · be persistent with relevance

## Localisation — global toolkit → local markets

One core toolkit of channel-agnostic assets that local markets adapt. What is fixed and what is flexible is marked here, because a market that is not told will decide for itself.

**Fixed.** the platform · the narrative · the do-not-say lines · a small global KPI set

**Flexible.** local hooks · spokespeople · language · local proof · market-specific tactics

## Measurement — wired in, not an afterthought

**Tagging.** Every asset uses one campaign identifier and urchin tracking module (UTM) format: up_stopline_[phase]_[audience]_[asset]_[channel]. Required fields are utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_content and utm_term when paid search is used.

**Cadence.** Paid activity is checked daily. Headline key performance indicators are reviewed weekly. The executive scorecard closes the programme at the end of Month 12.

**Levels.** Level 1 measures outputs: assets published, proof labels completed, partner packs delivered and approved claims linked to proof. Level 2 measures outtakes: comprehension score, message preference, trust lift, engagement quality and proof-page time on page. Level 3 measures outcomes: qualified meeting clicks, referred qualified leads, qualified inbound conversations, candidate interest and claim-compliance rate.

## Governance & the pre-publish gate

**Do not say.**
- Do not claim autonomous AI.
- Do not lead with a broad AI promise before approved proof exists.
- Do not use unapproved references.
- Do not make claim-level or AI-language approvals without Matthew Maday's technical confirmation.
- Do not imply AI owns delivery outcomes.
- Do not defend a broad AI promise when evidence is missing.
- Do not treat owner preference for control as settled buyer truth before message testing.
- Do not celebrate automation alone.
- Do not inflate refusal to do harmful work into a broad ethics platform.

**Legal and disclosure.** Before anything publishes, Kamen Kamenov gives final sign-off on positioning, proof lane, claims and public references. Matthew Maday gives technical confirmation for claim-level and AI-language approvals before release.

**The pre-publish checklist.** Self-contained · every phase has its objective, audience, messages and activities · message tracks are audience-specific with insight, benefit and proof · the collateral library is complete and on-template · fixed vs flexible is clear · measurement is wired in · governance is in place · versioned for distribution.

**Crisis tripwire.** Litigation, disclosure, deal, restructuring, life-safety and regulatory triggers escalate to a senior person before anything publishes.

**Data and AI.** Material non-public information never enters AI tools; #noAI defaults apply for restricted clients.

## Execution logistics — how the work actually runs

### The content lifecycle

- **CREATE** — brief & produce assets from the toolkit templates
- **ROLL OUT** — publish per the calendar, across PESO (Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned)
- **AMPLIFY** — boost reach, activate influencers & advocates
- **LISTEN & RESPOND** — monitor, run the newsroom, optimise on live signals

**Roles (RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed).** Who briefs, creates, approves, publishes and reports each asset. **Always-on newsroom:** a standing team for real-time stories and issues. **Approvals:** the sign-off path (incl. legal / client) before anything publishes.

No names are recorded against these roles. They are the client's to assign.

## Open — waiting on a person

- **Are these assets and these do-not-say lines approved?** — not yet; no owner recorded.
- **Who holds each RACI role?** — not yet assigned.

evaluation_narrative.finding: The campaign is pre-launch, so no objective can be judged yet. The first judgement comes after proof, trust, founder visibility and sales readings are live.
The Stop Line can be reported as contributed to qualified enterprise leads only when sales records show a campaign touchpoint before qualification and sales confirms the lead definition.
Outputs will show whether proof and claims were prepared correctly. Outtakes and outcomes will show whether buyers understood and trusted the story.
Audience and market differences will be read against each group's own starting point, not against another market's number.
No activity has worked yet because the campaign has not launched. The first working evidence will come from proof-page use, message-test results, founder-content response and qualified inbound.
Nothing has underperformed yet because no campaign result exists. Pre-launch risk sits in missing baselines, unapproved proof and unresolved public-profile conflicts.

Change the launch order only if proof, profile cleanup or baseline setup is not ready. Scale only the activity that meets its target, and stop any claim that cannot show proof, senior owner and limit.

Confidence is limited until baseline readings exist. Next time, set buyer and owner baselines before platform selection, confirm sales tracking before creative work starts, and agree the proof-asset target before the proof page is drafted.

non_negotiables: Do not use Advertising Value Equivalents
Do not present impressions as actual reach unless the data supports deduplication
Do not equate positive sentiment with behaviour or business impact
Do not aggregate markets without showing material local differences
Do not optimize solely for the easiest metric to collect
Always show baseline, target, result and trend together
Always distinguish what UP delivered, what audiences did, and what changed for the client
Preserve definitions, query logic and tagging conventions so results are repeatable
End every report with decisions and next actions, not merely observations

# Measurement & Evaluation Framework

Start from the business change and work backwards. A metric that cannot be connected upward to an audience change or an organizational objective does not belong here.

**Not approved.** The organizational objective is a person's to approve, and no owner is recorded.

Acronyms used below: AMEC (Association for Measurement and Evaluation of Communication), KPI (key performance indicator), IEF (Integrated Evaluation Framework), and AVE (Advertising Value Equivalent).

## The AMEC (Association for Measurement and Evaluation of Communication) chain

Organizational objectives → Communication objectives → Inputs → Activities → Outputs → Outtakes → Outcomes → Impact.

## Objectives

### Organizational (at most 1)

- By 30 June 2027, increase qualified enterprise leads among buyers in the United States and the European Union from sales tracking starting at zero on 25 August 2026 to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter.

### Communication (at most 3)

- By 30 June 2027, increase recognition of The B Team as a proof-led artificial intelligence engineering partner among owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers from baseline not established; it will be set in the first message-testing wave before launch to the target set in that same wave.
- By 30 June 2027, increase trust in The Stop Line among sampled chief technology officers and architecture owners from baseline not established; it will be set in the first buyer interview or survey wave before launch to the target set in that same wave.
- By 30 June 2027, increase understanding of Signed by Humans among owners of midsize businesses from baseline not established; it will be set in the first owner message test before launch to the target set in that same test.

### Executive KPIs (at most 5)

- By 30 June 2027, increase approved proof assets for The Stop Line among public AI (artificial intelligence) claims from zero approved assets to the target set at the first client conversation.
- By 30 June 2027, decrease unresolved public-profile conflicts among buyer-facing public records from six unresolved conflict areas to zero before any public release ships.
- By 30 June 2027, increase technical-buyer trust in The Stop Line among sampled CTOs and architecture owners from baseline not established; it will be set in the first buyer research wave to the target set in that wave.
- By 30 June 2027, increase approved Signed by Humans founder visibility among buyer and talent audiences from Matthew Maday's sampled baseline of 2 to 5 reactions and 0 to 2 comments, with Kamen Kamenov's baseline set at his first post, to a lift above each founder's baseline over the first campaign period.
- By 30 June 2027, increase qualified enterprise leads connected to The Stop Line among United States and European Union buyers from sales tracking starting at zero on 25 August 2026 to two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter.

## Shared measurement concepts

The words below are shared with the other engagement document that names them, and every document that carries one of them must preserve the same one-line definition beside it, so the reader finds the same meaning under the same word wherever they read:

- **definition** — what is being measured, and how the number is worked out
- **baseline** — the number a target is checked against
- **target** — the number this engagement aims at
- **source** — where the number is read from
- **collection_frequency** — how often the number is read
- **owner** — the person responsible for the number

#### Qualified enterprise leads connected to The Stop Line

**Definition.** Counts qualified enterprise leads from United States and European Union buyers that sales records connect to The Stop Line proof page, Signed by Humans founder content, partner proof pack or approved referral language.

**Collection.** Monthly and at quarter end.  ·  **Breakdown.** By market, source route, buyer type, qualification status and campaign touchpoint.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes founder sales follow-up, UP campaign management, owned proof assets, partner capacity and enough channel activity to create qualified opportunities.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls campaign setup and reporting, while qualification, sales response, referrals and buyer decisions depend on The B Team, partners and the market.

**Attribution method.** The campaign is described as contributed to a lead only when the record shows a campaign touchpoint before qualification and sales confirms the lead met the agreed definition.  —  correlation with some controls — say 'contributed to'

**Known limitations.** This does not claim sole cause unless a stronger comparison or closed-loop sales model is later added.

#### Talent pull in Sofia

**Definition.** Counts qualified senior-engineering inbound from Sofia talent audiences tied to approved The Stop Line or Signed by Humans story assets.

**Collection.** Monthly.  ·  **Breakdown.** By source, role level, asset, referral route and qualification outcome.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes recruitment-review access, founder or team content, UP reporting time and enough approved talent-facing material to test the story.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls the message and reporting structure, while candidate interest depends on The B Team's recruitment activity and the Sofia talent market.

**Attribution method.** Talent movement is described as coinciding with campaign activity unless the candidate record names the campaign asset or referral route.  —  directional evidence without controls — say 'coincided with', never 'caused'

**Known limitations.** Talent interest does not prove hiring success or buyer trust.

## Reporting

**Baseline before launch.** Before launch, United Partners records the proof-library count, claim-compliance status, public-profile conflicts, founder-content baselines, buyer trust baseline, owner comprehension baseline, sales tracking setup and talent tracking setup. Any baseline not yet established is labelled that way and given a named first-read date.

**During the campaign.** During the campaign, the weekly report compares the headline key performance indicators with target and ends with the decision to scale, change or stop the activity that produced the reading.

**One-page executive scorecard.** The one-page after-campaign executive scorecard is produced within ten working days of the final campaign reading.

**Cadence.** Weekly reporting runs during launch activity, monthly reporting runs outside launch activity, and the quarter-end review checks whether The Stop Line and Signed by Humans contributed to the enterprise-lead target.

## The three checkpoints

- Measurement gate
- Optimization gate
- Learning gate

## Impact evaluation

Impact evaluation records the following as possible alternative explanations for any impact-level result, so the reading names what else could have moved the number before it credits the campaign:

- product changes
- price promotions
- competitor activity
- seasonality
- major news events

## Governance

| role | assigned to |
| --- | --- |
| Client lead | approvals |
| Account director | the brief and alignment |
| Strategy lead | baseline and methodology |
| Channel leads | tagging and collection |
| Analyst | data quality, dashboards and evaluation |
| Campaign lead | execution decisions |

## The non-negotiables

These are enforced, not recited.

- Do not use Advertising Value Equivalents
- Do not present impressions as actual reach unless the data supports deduplication
- Do not equate positive sentiment with behaviour or business impact
- Do not aggregate markets without showing material local differences
- Do not optimize solely for the easiest metric to collect
- Always show baseline, target, result and trend together
- Always distinguish what UP delivered, what audiences did, and what changed for the client
- Preserve definitions, query logic and tagging conventions so results are repeatable
- End every report with decisions and next actions, not merely observations

## How an objective is written

`By [date], increase/decrease [audience change] among [specific audience] from [baseline] to [target], contributing to [organizational objective]`

An objective not written this way cannot be measured, because at least one of the date, the change, the audience, the baseline, the target or the business goal is missing.

## The KPI ladder — the template to select from

A fill-in template, not a menu: the operator selects the right KPIs for this campaign. Every campaign carries measures on at least three levels, including one outtake or outcome.

| level | recommended core KPIs | supporting diagnostics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outputs | Quality coverage rate; key-message penetration | Volume, impressions, publication count, content produced, relevant audience reach |
| Outtakes | Message recall; understanding; positive consideration; trust/sentiment shift | Engagement rate, video completion, dwell time, comment themes |
| Outcomes | Qualified visits; enquiries; registrations; applications; stakeholder action | CTR (click-through rate), branded search, landing-page behaviour, downloads |
| Impact | Pipeline/revenue contribution; reputation shift; recruitment result; policy/societal progress | Cost per result, efficiency trend, client operational data |

### Quality coverage rate (replaces raw clipping totals)

Score each item against:

- priority outlet/influencer
- priority-audience relevance
- key-message inclusion
- positive or neutral tone
- brand/spokesperson prominence
- desired call to action
- original reporting vs syndication

Report both the percentage meeting the agreed threshold and the underlying criteria. Collapsing them into one unexplained proprietary score is the thing this replaces.

| Crisis communications | Response speed, message consistency, stakeholder coverage. Understanding, reassurance, misinformation penetration | Complaint behaviour, stakeholder support, recovery of positive/neutral conversation | Trust recovery, reduced customer loss, risk avoided |

The weekly report must drive action, not simply document activity.
