record.question: The EU AI Act, General Data Protection Regulation and buyer governance context make AI trust claims sensitive; what data-handling, model-use and human-review proof can The B Team show today?
record.finding:
Regulatory context. The B Team's own site claims Agentic AI Development, Workflow Automations and AI Company Upgrade services, so EU AI regulation is part of the operating context when work is placed on, used in, or affects people in the EU (https://thebteam.com/services; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers).
Regulatory context. The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and became generally applicable on 2 August 2026, while prohibited AI practices and AI literacy duties started on 2 February 2025 and general-purpose AI model obligations started on 2 August 2025 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).
Regulatory context. The AI literacy duty applies to providers and deployers of AI systems, and Commission Q&A says Article 4 already applies from 2 February 2025 with supervision and enforcement rules applying from August 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers).
Regulatory context. AI Act Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026 to certain generative and interactive AI systems and deepfakes, including duties to inform people when they interact directly with an AI system and to mark AI-generated or manipulated content (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-transparency-obligations).
Regulatory context. High-risk AI classification is not established for The B Team, but the Commission says high-risk areas include biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, migration, asylum and border control, with rules applying from 2 December 2027 for those areas and 2 August 2028 for regulated products (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems).
Regulatory context. Clutch reports a verified The B Team project involving facial-recognition photo features and Azure, so future public claims around biometric or image AI should be screened carefully instead of treated as ordinary web development proof (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems).
Regulatory context. GDPR applies to small and medium-sized enterprises that process personal data, with some obligations depending on whether processing is core to the business or likely to create risk for individuals (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/data-protection-explained_en).
Regulatory context. The European Commission says Standard Contractual Clauses can be used as a GDPR safeguard for transfers from the EU or EEA to third countries, which is material because The B Team serves both U.S. and European clients (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/standard-contractual-clauses-scc_en; https://thebteam.com/).
Regulatory context. The EU Data Act has applied since 12 September 2025, adding buyer context for data access, use and cloud contracts even where a small custom-development vendor is not the main regulated platform (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-act).
Regulatory context. Bulgaria amended its Cybersecurity Act on 13 February 2026 to transpose NIS2, with expanded scope, cybersecurity risk measures, supply-chain security, training, and incident reporting at 24 hours, 72 hours and one month for covered entities (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).
Regulatory context. The EU Cyber Resilience Act entered into force on 10 December 2024; its main obligations apply from 11 December 2027 and reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act).
Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act applies to software or hardware products with digital elements made available on the EU market, so direct scope for The B Team depends on whether it markets software under its own name or trademark rather than only providing bespoke development services (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).
Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to perform a cybersecurity risk assessment, keep technical documentation, provide support-period information, handle vulnerabilities and run conformity assessment before placing covered products on the EU market (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).
Regulatory context. The Cyber Resilience Act requires actively exploited vulnerability and severe-incident notices through the CRA reporting route, with 24-hour early warning, 72-hour main notice, and later final reports depending on the event (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary).
Regulatory context. The Commission's 2026 guidance for general-purpose AI model providers says only significant modifications to AI models trigger provider obligations, while minor modifications do not, so The B Team should distinguish model integration from model-provider activity in any public AI claim (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers).
Regulatory context. The same guidance says Commission enforcement powers for general-purpose AI provider obligations start on 2 August 2026, and providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers).
Regulatory context. The European Data Protection Board's AI-model opinion says anonymity must be assessed case by case, and an AI model is anonymous only where identification or extraction of personal data is very unlikely, which matters for AI projects using client, user or scraped data (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-opinion-on-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en).
Regulatory context. The same EDPB opinion says legitimate interest can support some AI development or deployment only if processing is strictly necessary and the rights-balancing test is met, and unlawfully processed development data can affect later use unless the model has been properly anonymized (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/edpb-opinion-on-ai-models-gdpr-principles-support-responsible-ai_en).
Regulatory context. DORA has applied from 17 January 2025 and requires financial entities to manage ICT risk, report incidents, test resilience and govern ICT third-party providers, so The B Team's finance-sector work may face buyer due-diligence demands even if direct DORA designation is not established (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/news/digital-finance-2024-12-19_en).
Regulatory context. The new EU Product Liability Directive entered into force on 8 December 2024, must be transposed by EU countries by 9 December 2026, and applies to products placed on the EU market from 9 December 2026. It is built for new technologies including artificial intelligence and covers damage including destruction or corruption of data, so The B Team should separate bespoke services from any software or AI product it places on the EU market (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/free-movement-sectors/liability-defective-products_en).
Regulatory context. The same EU Product Liability Directive seeks to ensure there is an EU-based liable party even where the manufacturer is outside the EU. This matters for The B Team's U.S.-Europe work because any claim about ownership, deployment, resale or support of AI software may affect who is treated as the liable economic operator (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/free-movement-sectors/liability-defective-products_en).
Regulatory context. The European Commission says a company using a third-party contact list for direct marketing must be able to show GDPR-compliant collection, respect objections, inform people at first contact, and comply with ePrivacy rules for email marketing. This is material to a proof-building plan that may use founder outreach, referral lists, events or CRM exports (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/information-business-and-organisations/legal-grounds-processing-data/can-data-received-third-party-be-used-marketing_en).
Regulatory context. The FTC says advertising claims must be truthful, not deceptive or unfair, and evidence-based, including for online advertising that sells software, apps or other services. This adds U.S. claim-risk context to The B Team's AI-forward message for U.S. buyers (https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing).
Regulatory context. The FTC says model-as-a-service companies may be liable if they break privacy commitments, including promises not to use customer data to train or update models through direct or indirect methods. This is relevant even if The B Team integrates third-party models, because U.S. buyers may ask how client data, prompts and outputs are handled across providers (https://www.ftc.gov/policy/advocacy-research/tech-at-ftc/2024/01/ai-companies-uphold-your-privacy-confidentiality-commitments).
Regulatory context. The B Team privacy-policy search result says, "We do not use your personal data for automated decision-making or profiling" with legal or similar significant effects. Independent public sources opened in this pass stayed silent on that claim, and the opened page did not expose a detailed data-processing agreement, subprocessor list or AI-data-use terms (https://thebteam.com/privacy-policy).
Regulatory context. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary and is meant to help organizations build trustworthiness into the design, development, use and evaluation of AI products, services and systems. NIST released a Generative AI profile on 26 July 2024 and updated that profile page on 8 April 2026, making NIST a likely buyer reference point for U.S.-facing AI governance proof (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework; https://www.nist.gov/publications/artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence).
Regulatory context. The B Team privacy-policy search result says the policy was dated 15 March 2026 and says the company is committed to protecting privacy under GDPR (https://thebteam.com/privacy-policy).
Regulatory context. The B Team privacy-policy search result says, “All third-party service providers are contractually bound to process your data only on our instructions and in compliance with the GDPR”; no independent public source opened in this pass corroborated those contracts (https://thebteam.com/privacy-policy).
Regulatory context. The European Accessibility Act covers products and services including computers and operating systems, banking services, e-books, and e-commerce, which matters when The B Team builds consumer-facing EU digital services for clients (https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/european-accessibility-act-eaa_en).
Regulatory context. The European Accessibility Act summary says the rules apply from 28 June 2025 to covered products and services (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/accessibility-of-products-and-services.html).
Regulatory context. The EU Cyber Solidarity Act entered into force on 4 February 2025 and aims to improve EU detection, preparation, and response to major cybersecurity threats and attacks (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-solidarity).
Regulatory context. The EU Cyber Solidarity Act includes a European Cybersecurity Alert System made of national and cross-border cyber hubs, which use AI and data analytics to detect threats and share warnings across borders (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-solidarity).

verdicts.because: It engages the finding by naming the EU AI Act and GDPR regulatory context and asking for The B Team-specific proof on data handling, model use, human review, and buyer governance tied to its AI services.

It directly uses the finding’s EU AI Act and GDPR regulatory context and asks for The B Team-specific proof on data handling, model use, and human review, which matches the finding’s claims about AI services, AI-data-use terms, model-provider distinctions, and buyer governance expectations.

record.finding:
Category context. The B Team sits in a crowded Bulgarian software category: the U.S. Country Commercial Guide says Bulgaria has about 10,000 ICT companies, 70 percent of which export, and calls Bulgaria a top ICT outsourcing destination (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).
Category context. The same U.S. guide says Bulgaria's ICT revenue rose 300 percent over seven years to EUR 2.5 billion and that software is the best-performing ICT segment after 16 years of EU membership (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).
Category context. The Manifest lists The B Team among Bulgarian software developers with 8 reviews, a 5.0 rating, 10-49 employees, Sofia location and 2017 establishment, while nearby listings include AI Agents and larger Sofia competitors such as Accedia and Scalefocus (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).
Category context. Clutch lists The B Team at $50-$99 per hour, 10-49 employees, Sofia, founded 2017, and service mix led by 43 percent web development and 15 percent custom software development, which supports the brief's warning that the public profile still reads more like software services than AI specialist (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).
Category context. Clutch independently corroborates delivery proof through a verified Taggable review: a March 2019 ongoing custom software engagement, $50,000 to $199,999 range, about $140,000 spent, Azure and APIs, facial-recognition photo features, and over 1 million photos processed (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).
Category context. H512 describes The B Team Ltd. as a software company serving U.S. clients in finance, retail, healthcare, entertainment and digital communications, with 30 employees worldwide and 20 in Bulgaria, which corroborates the supplied brief's sector range and headcount range (https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/).
Category context. Gartner's 2026 agentic-AI cycle says only 17 percent of organizations have deployed AI agents, while more than 60 percent expect to do so within two years, so demand is high but proof of real delivery is still scarce (https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/hype-cycle-for-agentic-ai).
Category context. Gartner says agentic AI is at the "Peak of Inflated Expectations" and that fully autonomous agents are not ready for most enterprise uses, which makes an unqualified AI-agent claim risky for a small vendor with thin public proof (https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/hype-cycle-for-agentic-ai).
Category context. Gartner predicted in August 2025 that 40 percent of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5 percent at the time, which supports The B Team's AI-market opportunity (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-08-26-gartner-predicts-40-percent-of-enterprise-apps-will-feature-task-specific-ai-agents-by-2026-up-from-less-than-5-percent-in-2025).
Category context. Gartner also predicts that by 2027, 40 percent of enterprises will demote or shut down autonomous AI agents because governance gaps are found only after production incidents, so The B Team's category proof should cover autonomy level, access limits, approvals, logs, rollback and ownership (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-26-gartner-says-applying-uniform-governance-across-ai-agents-will-lead-to-enterprise-ai-agent-failure).
Category context. McKinsey's 2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey says only about 30 percent of organizations reach maturity level three or higher in strategy, governance and agentic-AI controls, which makes trust architecture a buyer concern rather than a legal footnote (https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/tech-forward/state-of-ai-trust-in-2026-shifting-to-the-agentic-era).
Category context. record.question: Bulgaria's software market is mature and export-led; what Bulgarian, European or founder-led proof should The B Team use so it is not heard as another nearshore supplier?
record.finding:
Geopolitical context. The B Team's cross-border market is explicit because its site says it is headquartered in Sofia and serves clients across the United States and Europe, and its public contact footprint includes Sofia and Spain (https://thebteam.com/).
Geopolitical context. Bulgaria's position as an EU-based export ICT hub supports The B Team's nearshore story because the U.S. Country Commercial Guide says 70 percent of about 10,000 Bulgarian ICT companies are export-only (https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/bulgaria-information-and-communications-technologies).
Geopolitical context. The World Economic Forum's 2026 Global Risks Report says geoeconomic confrontation was selected as the top risk most likely to trigger a material global crisis in 2026, with state-based armed conflict next, making cross-border buyer trust and continuity proof material for a Bulgaria-based firm serving U.S. and EU clients (https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-risks-report-2026/digest/).
Geopolitical context. The same World Economic Forum report ranks misinformation and disinformation second and cyber insecurity sixth in the two-year outlook, and says adverse outcomes of AI rises from 30th in the two-year outlook to fifth in the 10-year outlook, which makes AI trust claims a live context risk (https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-risks-report-2026/digest/).
Geopolitical context. The European Commission's 2026 Digital Decade country report says Bulgaria has a dynamic ICT sector but that SME uptake of AI, cloud and data analytics remains limited, which gives The B Team an opportunity to stand out but also raises buyer proof expectations (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
Geopolitical context. The OECD says Bulgaria's AI policy is guided by a 2020 national strategy with pillars including infrastructure, education, research, data, sector innovation and ethical AI, but that the strategy lacks a clear action plan with implementation activities and timelines (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/progress-in-implementing-the-european-union-coordinated-plan-on-artificial-intelligence-volume-1_6d530a88-en/bulgaria_26e81b51-en.html).
Geopolitical context. The OECD also says Bulgaria has Discoverer and HEMUS supercomputing facilities running, Avitohol under development, INSAIT established in 2023, and BgGPT as the country's first open-source Bulgarian-language model, which supports a national AI ecosystem story around Sofia and Bulgaria (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/progress-in-implementing-the-european-union-coordinated-plan-on-artificial-intelligence-volume-1_6d530a88-en/bulgaria_26e81b51-en.html).
Geopolitical context. The European Commission adopted the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision on 10 July 2023, allowing personal data to flow freely from the EU to participating U.S. companies, which is material to The B Team's U.S. and Europe client base (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/eu-us-data-transfers_en).
Geopolitical context. The Commission published the first review of that adequacy decision on 9 October 2024, so transatlantic data-transfer assurance has an active review history rather than being a settled background assumption (https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/adequacy-decisions_en).
Geopolitical context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says the United States had 5,427 AI data centers and that nearly all leading AI chips depend on one Taiwanese foundry, while U.S. AI talent inflow has dropped 89 percent since 2017, making AI supply-chain and talent geography part of the context for an EU-based AI services partner (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).
Geopolitical context. Stanford's 2026 AI Index says national AI strategies and state-backed AI supercomputing are rising, but model production remains concentrated in the United States and China, which reinforces the need for a Sofia-based firm to state clearly whether it builds, adapts, integrates or governs third-party models (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report).
Geopolitical context. The European Commission's Apply AI Strategy is designed to strengthen EU technological sovereignty and boost AI adoption across Europe, especially among small and medium-sized enterprises. It also promotes a buy-European approach for the public sector and focuses on open-source AI solutions, which can support an EU-based vendor story but also raises questions about dependence on non-European models and cloud providers (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/apply-ai).
Geopolitical context. The Commission says 19 AI Factories and 13 antennas are being set up, with at least 9 new AI-optimised supercomputers planned to more than triple EuroHPC AI computing capacity. These facilities are open to European users across industry, research, academia and public authorities (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-factories).
Geopolitical context. CORDIS says the EU-funded BRAIN++ project will establish Bulgaria's first AI Factory and create a national hub for foundation-model development, adaptation and deployment. It says the project addresses gaps in computing infrastructure, specialised models, governance frameworks, talent development and cross-sector support (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101250707).
Geopolitical context. CORDIS says BRAIN++ plans four specialised models: a 175-billion-parameter Bulgarian-language BgGPT, RoboticsBG for manufacturing and logistics, FORSE for earth-observation use cases, and MEDBG for healthcare. It also plans COMPL-AI, a compliance framework aligned with the EU AI Act (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101250707).
Geopolitical context. The 2026 Digital Decade Eurobarometer says 74 percent of Bulgarians consider digital policy a high EU priority (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
Geopolitical context. The same Eurobarometer says 91 percent of Bulgarian respondents rank protecting online privacy and security as the top priority for the next decade (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
Geopolitical context. The same Eurobarometer says 76 percent of Bulgarian respondents agree AI development should be carefully regulated to ensure safety, even if that may constrain developers (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
Geopolitical context. The same Eurobarometer says Bulgarian concerns about generative AI are privacy and data protection at 34 percent, ethical issues or potential misuse at 32 percent, and accuracy or incorrect information at 31 percent (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
Geopolitical context. Bulgaria’s national Digital Decade roadmap has 60 measures with a total budget of EUR 2.19 billion, and 48 percent of those measures are set to expire by the end of 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
Geopolitical context. The same report says Bulgaria has an estimated 112 edge nodes and one unicorn in 2025 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).

verdicts.because: It directly uses the finding's Bulgaria export-led ICT hub/nearshore story and The B Team proof-expectation claim by asking what Bulgarian, European or founder-led proof can distinguish it from another nearshore supplier.
It engages the finding through Bulgaria being an export-led ICT hub, The B Team's Sofia/EU-to-U.S. nearshore positioning, and the need for proof to distinguish it from generic nearshore suppliers.

record.question: The B Team's reputation problem is not weak capability; it is that the public proof system has not caught up with the AI-era story the company now wants buyers to believe. The white space is a proof-first AI software partner that shows exactly where its AI claim is true, where its public record still proves enterprise software craft better than AI depth, and where larger peers compete through scale and broader proof libraries. The strategy should first make the company easier to trust, then make it more visible.
record.finding:
AI proof gap. The company's newer AI positioning is not matched by AI-specific Clutch service lines; Clutch lists web development at 43%, custom software development at 15%, e-commerce at 10%, low/no-code at 10%, web design at 10%, ERP consulting and system integration at 5%, IT staff augmentation at 5%, and IoT at 2% (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team). (bears on: Constraints, guardrails & AI permissions)
Positioning-history pattern. The public-positioning trail now shows at least three eras: the older 'Offshore Like Next Door' platform, the 14 October 2022 website relaunch around that idea, and the 2026 AI-first site language (banked findings; https://thebteam.com/news; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real; https://thebteam.com/). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)
Each peer's share of voice. The B Team has 8 Clutch reviews, 10-49 employees, and a $50-$99 hourly rate. Clutch lists its common project size as $50,000-$199,999 based on 7 reviews (https://clutch.co/profile/b-team).
Each peer's share of voice. Lexis Solutions has 32 Clutch reviews, 10-49 employees, and appears on Clutch's Top Artificial Intelligence Companies in Sofia page with 25% AI consulting and 10% AI development. Its visible review count is four times The B Team's count (https://clutch.co/bg/developers/artificial-intelligence/sofia; https://clutch.co/profile/lexis-solutions).
Each peer's share of voice. Dreamix has 36 Clutch reviews, 250-999 employees, and a most common Clutch project size of $200,000-$999,999. Its visible proof volume is much larger than The B Team's 8-review record (https://clutch.co/profile/dreamix).
Each peer's share of voice. Accedia has 40 Clutch reviews, 250-999 employees, and service lines including 20% custom software development, 20% web development, and 15% AI development. Its visible review count is five times The B Team's count (https://clutch.co/profile/accedia).
Each peer's share of voice. Scalefocus has 39 Clutch reviews, 250-999 employees, and reports 1000+ projects across 26 countries for more than 300 clients. Its public proof base is far larger than The B Team's visible proof base (https://clutch.co/profile/scalefocus).
Each peer's share of voice. The Manifest's Bulgaria software-development list gives Dreamix 36 reviews and places it above Accedia, Scalefocus and Lexis Solutions in the visible ranking. It also lists VistaJet as a Dreamix client, adding a named proof signal not in the banked record (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).
Each peer's share of voice. The Manifest's same list gives Accedia 40 reviews, Scalefocus 39 reviews and Lexis Solutions 32 reviews, while The B Team appears much later with 8 reviews. That repeats the banked pattern on a second directory: The B Team's visible proof base is smaller than each selected peer's (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).
Each peer's share of voice. The Manifest's “most new reviews in the past 12 months” table names Dreamix with 7 new reviews, Lexis Solutions with 5 new reviews and Scalefocus with 3 new reviews. The B Team does not appear in the visible top 13 for new reviews, so its review momentum also trails selected peers on that source (https://themanifest.com/bg/software-development/companies).
Each peer's share of voice. Clutch's Top 13 Sofia AI Consulting Firms page lists Lexis Solutions at number 2 with a 37.3/40 ability-to-deliver score, 19/20 reviews score, 10/10 clients-and-experience score and 8.3/10 market-presence score. The B Team, Dreamix, Accedia and Scalefocus did not appear in the page text searched in this pass, so Lexis has a clearer AI-consulting directory signal than the selected peer set there (https://clutch.co/bg/consulting/ai/sofia).
Each peer's share of voice. LinkedIn adds a clear visibility ladder among the selected peers: Scalefocus shows 46,212 followers, Dreamix 20,339, Accedia 9,226, and Lexis Solutions 1,611. The B Team shows 136 followers, so its company-channel reach trails all four selected peers by a wide margin (https://bg.linkedin.com/company/scalefocus; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/dreamix-ltd; https://www.linkedin.com/company/accedia; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/lexis-solutions; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real).
Each peer's share of voice. GoodFirms ranks Accedia first on its Bulgaria software-development list with 4.9 stars and 15 verified reviews. That gives Accedia a second ranking signal beyond Clutch and The Manifest, while GoodFirms does not surface The B Team in the visible result text opened here (https://www.goodfirms.co/directory/country/top-software-development-companies/bulgaria).
Each peer's share of voice. Apify gives Lexis Solutions a separate marketplace voice with 25 reviews and a 5.0 rating. That makes Lexis visible to buyers looking for scraping, data, and AI-enabled data work, not only to buyers searching agency directories (https://apify.com/partners/find/lexis-solutions).
Each peer's share of voice. Clutch's Bulgaria AI-development page was updated on August 20, 2026 and does not contain The B Team in the visible page text searched here (https://clutch.co/bg/developers/artificial-intelligence). The same page lists Lexis Solutions with 32 reviews, Dreamix with 36 reviews, Scalefocus with 39 reviews, and Accedia with 40 reviews (https://clutch.co/bg/developers/artificial-intelligence).
Each peer's share of voice. Clutch adds recent-review momentum for selected peers on the AI-development page: Lexis Solutions had 2 reviews in the past six months, Dreamix had 2 reviews in the past six months, and Scalefocus had 3 reviews in the past six months (https://clutch.co/bg/developers/artificial-intelligence).
Each peer's share of voice. Clutch adds buyer-footprint signals for selected peers: Dreamix has completed reviewed projects in 11 countries, Accedia in 10 countries, and Scalefocus shows experience in 14 industries (https://clutch.co/bg/developers/artificial-intelligence).
Each peer's share of voice. DesignRush gives Lexis Solutions another public review and portfolio channel: it shows 3 DesignRush reviews, 17 Google reviews, and named portfolio entries for Onnoplus, Finansi.bg, StaffSquared, FranceVerif and Mindance (https://www.designrush.com/agency/profile/lexis-solutions).
Public identity pattern. The banked record forms a new pattern: the public identity has three layers, with an AI-first current site, older software-services directory profiles, and Bulgarian registry records whose dates and addresses do not match the site narrative (banked findings: company site, H512, Clutch, Papagal, CompanyBook). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)
Public identity pattern. The banked record shows a domain and identity split across thebteam.com, yourbteam.com email addresses, yourbteam.net, LinkedIn's 'The B Team - Real' label, and older directory references to http://www.yourbteam.com; this is a new pattern from the banked findings, not a new source fact (banked findings: https://thebteam.com/; https://bg.linkedin.com/company/the-b-team-real; https://yourbteam.net/; https://dev.bg/company/the-b-team/; https://h512.com/company/the-b-team/). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

verdicts.because: The deciding facts are the AI proof gap, the three-era positioning history, smaller visible proof base, and larger peers' stronger scale/review signals; the rest is a permitted provisional judgement about what those facts mean.

The deciding facts are the AI proof gap, three-era positioning history, older software-service public profiles, and peers' larger review/reach/ranking signals, which reasonably support the claim's proof-system and visibility judgement.

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Two personas, convened on the Step 3 pair before the final-brief hard stop. The CFO asks where the business and the number are behind every measure; the Journalist asks which claim outruns the evidence the material actually supplies. The pair is adjudicated, not advised: a critical finding or a block from either stops the run before approval is even requested.

Convened on the Step 3 pair: The CFO / Board · The Journalist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The CFO / Board | So what — where's the business and the number? | PASS | 0 |
| The Journalist | Where's the substance? I'm going to check. | CONCERN | 1 |

## The findings

### 1. The Journalist — Medium

**Finding.** Success section requires founder visibility and talent pull tracking, but the Measurement Brief scorecard does not include a measure, source, collection frequency or owner for either.

**Quoted target.** "The scorecard sits in the measurement brief and must also track proof quality, founder visibility, search clarity and talent pull."

**Suggested fix.** Add scorecard rows for founder visibility and talent pull, or change the success line to only name dimensions actually measured in Step 3.

## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.

# Research & Insight Pack

One pack, not five disconnected audits. Every finding shows where it came from -- for a web finding, a URL (uniform resource locator); for supplied material, the place in the pack it came from. A finding this engine could not source from the material it was given says so in its own row rather than being presented as research. The AI (artificial intelligence) drafts each audit and a strategist validates and interprets it. The Sweet Spot the pack ends on names the client's USP (unique selling proposition) at the intersection with the insight nobody else has leveraged yet.

## Client Style Note

Captured from the client's own published communications. Every client-facing deliverable is written to this voice -- its tone, typical sentence length, vocabulary, self-reference, and signature do/don't words.

- **tone:** The client's owned voice is concise, technical and aspirational, with a craft-and-AI contrast at its center.
- **sentence length:** Sentences are mostly short to medium, with one clear claim per line or paragraph.
- **vocabulary:** The vocabulary combines engineering terms with human delivery language: AI development, enterprise-grade software, automation, architect-led delivery, craft, workflow and fit.
- **self reference:** The client refers to itself as The B Team and uses first-person plural sparingly through service and contact language.
- **signature do words:** AI, craftsmanship, enterprise-grade, architect-led, hand-crafted, agentic AI, workflow automations, fit
- **signature dont words:** cheap offshore, best-in-class, game-changing, world-class, revolutionary, full-service agency, marketing activation
- **sources:** https://thebteam.com/, https://thebteam.com/about, https://thebteam.com/services, https://thebteam.com/process, https://thebteam.com/case-studies, https://thebteam.com/privacy-policy
- **long form voice:** Not yet calibrated: no long-form writing of the client's own has been read.
- **voice evidence read:** short-form copy only — long-form voice not yet calibrated

## Clear, professional communication language

Every Research document meets the clear, professional communication language standard. The wording is checked sentence by sentence and the whole text is checked end to end, against the rules named in the language standard.

**Wording rules**
- **Plain words:** Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
- **Short sentences:** One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
- **Concrete, not abstract:** Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
- **Proof, not adjectives:** Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
- **Confident, not inflated:** Assured, warm but not casual, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
- **One name per thing:** Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
- **Reader's language, not the method's:** Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's. No process term reaches a client page unexplained.

**Whole-text rules**
- **One clear purpose:** The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
- **Headline first:** Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the story.
- **Logical flow:** Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
- **Right length:** As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
- **Short paragraphs:** One idea per paragraph. If a paragraph runs long, split it. A wall of text goes back.
- **Visual clarity:** Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
- **Self-contained:** A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.

## Accountable review gates

Research writes the assignment on every pack so the discipline check reads a real owner next to every gate that reviews its output.

| review gate | accountable owner |
| --- | --- |
| Research pack review | United Partners strategy lead |
| Sourcing & figures audit | United Partners quality lead |
| Insight review board | United Partners head of insight |

## Primary reputation risks

Research names the primary reputation risks on every pack so the discipline check reads them against the work rather than inferring them from adjacent context.

- overclaim
- inconsistency
- ambiguity

## Do not say

Research works only from the material it was handed. The three shapes of invention the pack refuses are named here, each with why the pack refuses it.

| do not say | why |
| --- | --- |
| invented clients | Research works only from the material it was handed; a client relationship, quote or reference the material does not carry cannot be attributed to a client. |
| invented metrics | No number, percentage, ranking or share of voice enters the pack unless a source in the supplied material carries it. No invented figures, at all, for any reason. |
| invented claims | A statement about the market, the audience or the client is only Research when a source in the supplied material grounds it. A finding Research could not source says so in its own row rather than being presented as a claim. |

## Executive summary

What a reader gets if they read nothing else. Each finding carries what it changes.

1. **The B Team's owned site now presents the company as an artificial intelligence development company in Sofia, but the strongest third-party record still presents it mainly as software and web delivery.**
   _no date recorded_ · source: https://thebteam.com/; https://clutch.co/profile/b-team · confidence: high · directional — not fact
   **So what.** The strategy should not ask buyers to accept the artificial intelligence story on language alone. It should first connect the new claim to proof assets that a buyer can check.

2. **The public record carries unresolved conflicts on founding year, headcount, address, legal name and domain identity.**
   _26 August 2026; 2026-08-19_ · source: Approved Brief, Step 1 Briefing Pack and https://papagal.bg/eik/203913310/d653 · confidence: high
   **So what.** The strategy must treat consistency as a trust move, not a housekeeping task. These fields should be settled before buyer-facing material goes public.

3. **Client reviews give The B Team a strong proof base for craft, delivery and client trust.**
   _no date recorded_ · source: https://clutch.co/profile/b-team · confidence: high · directional — not fact
   **So what.** The strategy should turn directory-held proof into owned proof, because the best evidence now sits on third-party review pages rather than in The B Team's own proof library.

4. **Selected peers already support artificial intelligence positioning with stronger public proof routes, including review volume, awards, product pages, marketplace listings and named case evidence.**

   **So what.** The B Team's ownable space is not scale. It is proof-first, founder-led, governed artificial intelligence delivery with clear limits on claims.

5. **European Union artificial intelligence transparency duties under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026 for certain artificial intelligence systems and content uses.**

   **So what.** The B Team's governed artificial intelligence claim should include plain buyer proof on disclosure, human review, data handling and claim limits where relevant.

## Card 1

**Owners are not buying AI because it sounds advanced. They are buying a calmer way to see work, risk and responsibility before problems become expensive.**

**Type.** intuitive

**The 5 T's.** True: pass — The approved brief names owners of midsize businesses as the primary audience and says they want more control and visibility. · Tacit: pass — It names the quieter buyer motive beneath the AI language: less surprise, clearer work and safer responsibility. · Touches the heart: partial — It reaches anxiety about control, but the research register is trust-led rather than emotionally warm. · Tension: pass — It sets the market's AI-speed story against the buyer's need for control and proof. · Triggers action: pass — It tells the strategy to lead with visibility, checks and ownership before AI claims.

**The tension.** The market sells AI as speed and capability. Elena needs control, visibility and someone senior to own the outcome.

**The audience it is about.** Owners of midsize businesses who want more control and visibility without becoming technical buyers themselves.
**Audience personas.** Elena

**The opportunity it opens.** The B Team can own a proof-first AI story for owners who distrust vague automation claims but still want the benefit of better systems.

**Evidence.** The approved brief names owners of midsize businesses as the primary audience and says they want more control and visibility. The research also shows that The B Team's strongest proof is trusted software delivery, while its AI proof still needs to be built and approved.

**So what.** The strategy should lead with controlled work, visible checks and accountable delivery. AI should be explained as the system behind that control, not as the headline claim.

# The extraction process — seven steps

1. Immerse — absorb the research pack, the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation read
2. Generate volume — write many candidates, empirical and intuitive; do not edit yet
3. So-What ladder — push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated 'so what?'
4. Screen — test each against the five T's and discard what fails any of them
5. Find the Sweet Spot — the ownable truth, an insight not yet leveraged, what the audience truly cares about
6. Distinctiveness Gate — reject anything a competitor could also claim, or the obvious white space everyone sees
7. Distil — land one to three Killer Insights, no more

# Two kinds of insight — and why you need both

| --- | --- | --- |
| Empirical insight | Grounded in data acquired through research methods | The data itself |
| Intuitive insight | Grounded in knowing or sensing, without a rational process | Observation and qualitative evidence — it still needs backup |

**The UP principle.** It is through science that we prove, but through intuition that we discover. The strongest Killer Insights pair an intuitive human truth with empirical proof — the discovery and the evidence together.

# The climb — from data to insight

Insight is a level on a ladder, reached by disciplined questioning — not a lucky thought.

| level | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| Data | Raw, uncontextualised facts ("sales rose 23%") |
| Information | Data organised & compared ("23% — 5 points above target, 8 below history") |
| Insight | What it means, strategically ("the growth is masking a loyalty problem") |
| Foresight | What it signals for the future ("expect margin pressure in 12 months") |

**The tool that climbs it: the So What? test.** For every finding ask "so what?" and keep asking until you reach genuine meaning. Guard against the five traps:

- correlation mistaken for causation
- confirmation bias
- volume mistaken for significance
- the missing counterfactual
- outliers mistaken for trends

# The Sweet Spot

An insight sits where all three meet:

- the company's ownable truth
- an insight not yet leveraged
- what the audience truly cares about

# Step 5B · Validate the insight

A distinctive, contrarian insight cannot lock until it is tested against the real audience. Distinctiveness and wrongness look identical until tested.

## Validating card 1

**How contrarian.** This cuts against the market belief that an AI repositioning should lead with bigger AI capability claims. It also challenges The B Team to treat restraint and visibility as the offer, not as caveats around the offer.

**What would validate it.** Ask owners of midsize businesses to compare two messages: one led by AI development capability and one led by control, visibility, checks and accountable delivery. The insight is confirmed if they say the control-led message makes them more willing to take a meeting. It is refined if they like the control promise but need more technical proof or sector examples. It is rejected if they prefer the AI-capability message and do not see control as a meaningful reason to consider The B Team.

**Verdict.** Confirm · Refine · Reject — none recorded. The test has not been run.


# Open — waiting on a person

- **Which of these is the insight?** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.
- **What did the audience say?** — the validation test has not been run, so no verdict is recorded.

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Three personas, convened at step 5B against the insight alone, to kill a weak insight before a whole strategy is built on it. The Competitor asks whether they could claim it word for word, the Target Audience whether they recognise themselves in it, the Activist what it looks like turned over. It is not the pre-ship board and it does not clear the work; it stops one thing from being built on.

Convened at step 5B: The Competitor · The Target Audience · The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Competitor | I can say that too. | PASS | 0 |
| The Target Audience | Why do I care? I don't believe you. | PASS | 0 |
| The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist | Here's how this blows up. | CONCERN | 2 |

## The findings

### 1. The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist — Medium

**Finding.** The competitor contrast creates an avoidable counter-attack because named peers could challenge the claim that they cannot match the restraint position.

**Quoted target.** "Lexis Solutions, Dreamix, Accedia and Scalefocus can answer with governed delivery language, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder sign-off, approved-reference path, internal proof route and public refusal to overclaim unchanged."

**Suggested fix.** Keep the insight, but rewrite the peer contrast as an internal ownability claim until competitor proof has been checked line by line: The B Team can make restraint ownable through founder sign-off, approved references, internal proof and refusal to overclaim.

### 2. The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist — Medium

**Finding.** The insight names public refusal to overclaim as a differentiator, which can become a target if critics ask for examples of refused claims or harmful work boundaries.

**Quoted target.** "public refusal to overclaim AI"

**Suggested fix.** Before building the strategy on this, define the refusal boundary in practical terms: what The B Team will not claim, what work it declines, who approves exceptions, and what proof is publishable.

## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.

# Strategy One-Pager

The one page everything else flows from. A gap here is a gap in the thinking.

**No approach has been chosen.** The options are below with their evaluation; the choice belongs to a person and no owner is recorded.

Engagement tier: standard-enterprise — the ten boxes of this page are the complete set for this tier.

Claim boundary: Kamen Kamenov gives final sign-off on positioning, proof lane, claims and public references. Matthew Maday gives technical confirmation for claim-level and AI-language approvals before release.

Concept boundary: The fixed concept is proof-first restraint: The B Team makes AI credible by showing evidence, senior responsibility and limits. In public, it should be shown through approved proof, demonstrations, references and stop lines, not proclaimed as a superiority claim.

## Executive summary (2–3 lines)

The strategy should make restraint visible before The B Team promotes its artificial intelligence (AI) story.

It speaks first to Elena, the owner who wants more control and visibility without becoming technical.

The public story should show approved proof, senior responsibility and clear limits before it asks buyers to believe the AI claim.

## Business & communication objectives (SMART+I)

Communication objective: By 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027), make owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers see The B Team as a proof-led artificial intelligence (AI) engineering partner by publishing only approved, traceable AI claims and lifting buyer trust, proof credibility and founder visibility above their first recorded baselines.

Business objective: Win two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union by 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027).

## Target audience profile & persona

Target audience profile & persona: The strategy leads with owners of midsize businesses who want control and visibility, then equips technical buyers, including chief technology officers and architecture owners, with proof. It also supports senior Sofia talent with a craft-led AI story. Persona: Elena.

## The strategic approach + one-line positioning

Approach: Proof-first restraint.

Positioning: The B Team makes AI credible by showing the proof, the people responsible and the line it will not cross.

Positioning (lead line): Restraint is the proof.

**Positioning (lead line).** Restraint is the proof.

**Expression options for the person to choose from.** The concept is fixed; the public expression is open. Candidates: “Proof before promise” (restraint before promotion), “Where AI stops, trust starts” (visible limits as trust), “Senior-owned AI delivery” (human responsibility behind AI). The choice belongs to a person and is tested with the audience before public use.

**It holds only if.** The recommended approach is believable only if the proof library, public identity cleanup and claim approval route are visible before public AI promotion. Buyers must be able to see what is proved, who owns the claim and where AI stops. If that condition fails, restraint stops looking like discipline and starts looking like a claim without proof.

## Core narrative & 3–5 key messages

Core narrative: The B Team is not asking buyers to trust AI because it sounds fast or advanced. It asks them to trust AI-supported delivery only where senior people govern the work, approve the claim and show where the system stops.

Key messages: AI supports the work; senior people still own the outcome. Every public AI claim must connect to approved proof. The B Team will not claim autonomous AI. The proof comes before the promotion. Clear limits make the AI story easier to trust.

## Proof points / supporting evidence

The approved brief says The B Team claims governed, checked and reviewable AI, never autonomous AI. The approved brief says Kamen Kamenov signs positioning, proof lane, claims and public references. The approved brief says Matthew Maday confirms claim-level and AI-language approvals before release. The research pack says The B Team's strongest public proof is trusted software delivery, while public AI proof still needs to be built and approved. The measurement brief says proof assets must be marked as named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.

## Channel strategy (PESO)

Paid, Earned, Shared and Owned (PESO) shape: earned activity leads once the proof library and public identity cleanup are ready, because the reputation gap needs independent credibility. Owned proof pages and founder-led shared posts prepare the evidence; paid activity supports targeted testing and retargeting only.

**Why this leads.** Earned media leads because the gap is credibility, not reach. Owned and shared channels can state the proof, but independent validation makes the repositioning harder to dismiss.

## Campaign timeline & phases

No delivery date is established beyond 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027). The practical order is public identity cleanup, proof library lock, message testing, founder-led proof launch and earned validation.

**The phasing spine.** 1) Clean the public identity. 2) Lock the proof library. 3) Test the control-led message. 4) Launch founder-led proof. 5) Earn third-party validation.

## Success metrics & KPIs

Measurement follows the Association for Measurement and Evaluation of Communication Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the Integrated Evaluation Framework. Core measures are proof credibility, technical-buyer trust, public-profile consistency, founder visibility and talent pull in Sofia.

## Budget allocation summary · risk mitigation

The pilot runs at United Partners' internal cost, and out-of-pocket costs are decided case by case. The main risks are an AI story that outruns proof, public identity inconsistency, unapproved references and unclear data or AI claims.

**Issues preparedness.** Under public or buyer challenge, the approach holds because it carries fewer claims and each claim has an approval route and proof type. If evidence is missing, the message narrows instead of defending a broad AI promise.

# The Strategy Blueprint cascade

Everything in line of sight: business objective → communication objective → strategic approach → narrative → messages → pillars → platform → tactics → KPIs.

**Business objective.** Win two qualified enterprise leads per calendar quarter from buyers in the United States and the European Union by 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027).

**Communication objective (SMART+I).** By 30 June 2027 (the second quarter of 2027), make owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers see The B Team as a proof-led artificial intelligence (AI) engineering partner by publishing only approved, traceable AI claims and lifting buyer trust, proof credibility and founder visibility above their first recorded baselines.

**How it traces.** The communication objective serves the business objective by giving qualified buyers a clear, proved reason to trust the AI story and take a meeting before the lead target date.

# The decision rule

If a message cannot show the approved proof behind the AI claim, the senior owner responsible for it and the line the system will not cross, it does not ship.

The team's day-to-day test for whether a message belongs.

# The options it was chosen from

Weak strategy is the first plausible approach written up confidently. These are the alternatives and how each scored.

## Option 1 — Proof-first restraint

**Shape.** Own the tension

**Direction.** GET owners of midsize businesses, technical buyers and senior Sofia talent WHO see AI claims as easy to overstate TO see The B Team as the AI engineering partner that proves what it claims BY making every public claim traceable to approved proof, senior ownership and visible limits.

**Positioning.** The B Team makes AI credible by showing the proof, the people responsible and the line it will not cross.

# UP's recommendation

It is strongest across fit, distinctiveness, feasibility and durability because it answers the core tension with a proof route The B Team can actually operate. It also gives the other two routes a role without letting either narrow the strategy too early.

compose-big-idea.output:
# The Creative Big Idea

Built through the IdeaHaus method — creativity with structure. A Big Idea is the single organising thought that makes an audience feel something and act, and that a whole programme of work can hang from for years. It is the elevated purpose; a tactic is the activity that serves it. The most common creative failure is presenting the second dressed as the first.

12 candidates were generated and 2 were marked as tactics rather than ideas. 3 are built out below.

**No idea has been chosen.** The volume gives the creative spark and the taste to a person, and no owner is recorded.

## The elevated objective

**What the client asked for.** The B Team needs a campaign idea that makes its artificial intelligence story credible to owners of midsize businesses and technical buyers without overstating what AI can do.

**The value we add.** United Partners turns restraint from a safety caveat into a public trust signal: proof, senior responsibility and a visible line that AI does not cross.

**Elevated (NEED + VALUE = POWER).** Make The B Team the company that changes how ambitious businesses judge AI partners: not by who promises the most automation, but by who can show the proof, the people responsible and the line where the system stops.

**Result-back (the movie ending).** On launch day, owners, technical buyers and peers are pointing to The B Team's line in the sand and asking their own partners where AI stops and human responsibility begins. The campaign has succeeded when the market repeats the demand: show me the proof, show me the person and show me the stop line.

## The insights

**AI becomes more credible for The B Team when restraint is visible, because the buyer's real fear is not weak technology; it is losing control of responsibility, evidence and judgement.** (intuitive) — This follows from the approved brief's proof-first restraint position and the audience hypothesis that owners value control and visibility without becoming technical buyers.

| T | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| True | Pass: it fits the approved strategy and the stated audience concern. |
| Tacit | Pass: it names restraint as the hidden trust signal beneath AI interest. |
| Touches the heart | Partial: it reassures anxious owners, but the emotional pull still needs audience testing. |
| Tension | Pass: it sets market AI ambition against the need for limits. |
| Triggers action | Pass: it points directly to proof assets, claim approval and visible stop lines. |

**A smaller AI claim can feel stronger than a larger one when the proof is cleaner, the owner is visible and the limit is explicit.** (empirical) — The research pack says The B Team's strongest public proof is trusted software delivery, while public AI proof still needs to be built and approved.

| T | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| True | Pass: the evidence supports a narrower public claim route. |
| Tacit | Pass: it reveals why restraint can feel like confidence. |
| Touches the heart | Partial: it builds trust, but it may need a sharper human story to move beyond reassurance. |
| Tension | Pass: it challenges the category instinct to sound bigger. |
| Triggers action | Pass: it directs the launch to fewer claims and better evidence. |

## The three built out

A true Big Idea is also: about the brand's purpose/benefit; stands out in its category; radically opens hearts and minds; creates movement.

### The Stop Line

**In one sentence.** The B Team makes AI credible by publicly showing the point where automation stops and senior human responsibility takes over.

**The elevated purpose.** Change the buyer's question from 'what can your AI do?' to 'where does your AI stop, and who is responsible after that?'

**Why it works.** It turns the client's proof-first restraint into a memorable market demand that competitors can discuss but cannot copy with the same founder sign-off, approved claim route and refusal to overclaim.

**The movement it creates.** Owners ask for a stop line before they trust an AI partner; technical buyers test claims against proof; institutions and peers borrow the language to demand clearer limits.

**Why it meets the IdeaHaus bar.** It meets the IdeaHaus bar because it is about The B Team's benefit, stands out from inflated AI promises, opens hearts through reassurance and creates movement by giving buyers a question to ask.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Simple | Pass: the idea is easy to repeat because it turns trust into one concrete image, a line that AI does not cross. |
| Shareable | Pass: 'show me the stop line' gives buyers, founders and technical leaders a phrase they can use in posts, sales conversations and scrutiny. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can stretch from a website line to proof pages, demos, events, sales tools and earned media. |
| Memorable | Pass: the phrase is visual and contrasts sharply with the category's usual speed and capability language. |
| Ownable | Pass: competitors can claim governance, but they cannot copy The B Team's founder approval route, proof library and public refusal to overclaim unchanged. |
| Persuasive | Pass with a condition: it persuades only if every public claim links to approved proof and a named human approval route. |

### Signed by Humans

**In one sentence.** Every AI claim from The B Team carries visible human ownership before it reaches the market.

**The elevated purpose.** Make human responsibility the proof mark that separates serious AI delivery from loose automation talk.

**Why it works.** It makes the abstract promise of governance feel personal, accountable and repeatable by showing that a senior person approves the claim before the market sees it.

**The movement it creates.** Buyers start asking who signed the claim; teams attach human approval to AI work; public proof shifts from system capability to accountable responsibility.

**Why it meets the IdeaHaus bar.** It meets the IdeaHaus bar because it carries the brand benefit, opens hearts through accountability and creates a visible behavior people can copy or demand.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Simple | Pass: the idea is clear in three words and needs little explanation. |
| Shareable | Pass: it works as a public prompt, proof mark and launch expression. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can appear on claim pages, case studies, technical artifacts, demos and leadership posts. |
| Memorable | Pass: it gives the campaign a human signature in a category full of machine language. |
| Ownable | Partial: the phrase is strong for The B Team, but another firm could imitate the signature device unless The B Team ties it tightly to its approval route and proof library. |
| Persuasive | Pass: it makes accountability visible and lowers the risk of vague AI claims. |

### Fewer Promises, Better Proof

**In one sentence.** The B Team earns trust by making fewer AI claims and proving each one more clearly.

**The elevated purpose.** Make restraint feel like confidence: a company that can prove its claims does not need to inflate them.

**Why it works.** It attacks the category habit of sounding bigger and gives The B Team a disciplined way to launch before its public AI proof is fully mature.

**The movement it creates.** Buyers reward evidence over volume; sales conversations narrow to what can be proved; the company cuts any claim that has no approved proof type.

**Why it meets the IdeaHaus bar.** It meets part of the IdeaHaus bar because it supports the brand benefit and stands apart from overclaiming, but it is more strategic discipline than full emotional platform.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Simple | Pass: the sentence is plain and immediately understandable. |
| Shareable | Partial: it is easy to quote, but it has less public drama than The Stop Line or Signed by Humans. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can guide messaging, proof assets, media interviews and sales enablement. |
| Memorable | The thought is strong, but the wording is harder to make yours and less easy to picture than the platform wording already approved for use. |
| Ownable | Weak: disciplined proof is credible for The B Team, but many competitors could claim a similar stance. |
| Persuasive | Pass: it turns the client's limited public AI proof into a disciplined trust position. |

## The volume it came from

Creativity without structure is chaos. Every candidate below names the trainer that produced it, and whether it is really an idea or a tactic — the mayonnaise-versus-sandwich test.

| candidate | trainer | idea or tactic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Stop Line | Challenge Idea | idea |
| Signed by Humans | Movement | idea |
| Where AI Stops, Trust Starts | Provocation | idea |
| The Receipts Before the Robot | Random Entry | idea |
| No Claim Leaves Alone | Movement | idea |
| The Human Approval Layer | Provocation | tactic |
| Fewer Promises, Better Proof | Challenge Idea | idea |
| The Line We Will Not Cross | Provocation | idea |
| Proof Has a Signature | Random Entry | idea |
| Show the Stop | Challenge Idea | tactic |
| AI With an Adult in the Room | Provocation | idea |
| Every Claim Has an Owner | Movement | idea |

## The six IdeaHaus steps, as applied

1. Internalize the strategy — The work starts from proof-first restraint, with AI made credible through approved proof, senior responsibility and visible limits.
2. Result-back thinking — The campaign ending is a market behavior: buyers ask every AI partner to show the proof, the person responsible and the stop line.
3. Embrace insights — The WHO truths are that owners may value control and visibility more than AI capability language (intuitive), and the approved brief supports governed, checked and reviewable AI rather than autonomous AI (empirical).
4. Elevate the objectives — The objective moves from promoting The B Team's AI story to changing how buyers judge responsible AI partners.
5. Focused ideation — The four trainers produced headlines that forced restraint, signatures, proof and limits into campaign-scale ideas rather than claim checks alone.
6. Validate against the Big Idea Criteria — The built ideas were tested for simplicity, shareability, scale, memory, ownership, persuasion and their ability to create real buyer movement.

## Validation against the IdeaHaus Big Idea Criteria

The eight criteria, applied to the recommended direction. Where a criterion is only partly met, it is marked so — the check must discriminate.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| About the brand's purpose/benefit | Pass: The Stop Line expresses The B Team's benefit as governed AI delivery with senior responsibility and proof. |
| Stands out in its category | Pass: it rejects the category's usual speed and capability race and makes visible restraint the trust signal. |
| Radically opens heart & mind | Pass with a condition: it can change how buyers feel about AI risk, but only if the proof feels human and not procedural. |
| Simple | Pass: the idea is short, visual and easy to repeat. |
| Scalable | Pass: it can scale across positioning, website, proof library, demos, sales tools, founder content and earned media. |
| Recognisable, memorable asset | Pass: the stop line is a repeatable verbal and visual asset. |
| Creates movement | Pass: it gives buyers a concrete demand: show me where AI stops and who takes responsibility. |
| Shareable, any-size screen | Partial: the phrase travels well, but the proof detail behind it must be simplified for small-screen use. |

**The claim guardrail still holds.** The idea can be big, but every claim stays small enough to prove. Public AI language must remain governed, checked and reviewable, with each claim tied to approved proof, a responsible human and a clear line the system does not cross; the bigger the platform becomes, the more important that proof discipline becomes.

## Two conditions carried into execution

1 · **Proof before public scale.** No public AI claim ships unless it is approved and tied to one proof type: named reference, verifiable anonymous reference, technical artifact or internal demo.

2 · **Human ceiling for emotional altitude.** A named human owner must protect the emotional height of The Stop Line and Signed by Humans when they become pages, posts, demos and sales tools, so the work does not collapse into proof mechanics alone.


## The Big Idea

One of the three above becomes the Big Idea. Which one is not recorded here, because the volume gives that choice to a person.

## Open — waiting on a person

- **Which idea has the heart?** — not yet chosen; no owner recorded.

# Message Architecture

One connected architecture, not three separate lists. Every message and every pillar traces back to the one story; anything that does not, does not belong.

**Waiting on an owner.** The story's truth and its tension belong to a person, and no owner has approved them in writing yet.

## Rebuilt from the Big Idea

This architecture is built from the Big Idea the strategist decided — The Stop Line, launched through Signed by Humans — not from the nearest provable frame. The idea's role is the spine; the first-believer audience is the first proof of it, not the whole story.

## The narrative

**World.** Artificial intelligence (AI) has made software claims easier to make and harder to trust. Owners want the benefit, but they need to see who is responsible, what is proved and where the system stops.

**Tension.** The market pulls AI stories toward speed and capability. The B Team's credible ground pulls the other way: fewer claims, approved proof, senior responsibility and visible limits.

**Resolution.** The tension resolves when restraint becomes the trust signal. The B Team leads with The Stop Line, so every AI claim shows the proof behind it, the people responsible for it and the limit it will not cross.

**Our role.** The B Team's role is to make governed AI believable by making the stop line public, provable and Signed by Humans.

### In the UP template

**We believe in a world where…** AI-supported delivery should be useful without becoming vague, hidden or unowned.

**We know…** Buyers do not need a bigger AI promise. They need proof they can inspect, senior people they can hold accountable and a clear line the system will not cross.

**So we make sure…** Every public AI claim is approved, traceable and limited to what The B Team can prove.

**Which is why we…** Work from The Stop Line: proof first, senior ownership visible and every claim Signed by Humans.

### Compressed

**Trailer.** Elena wants the control and visibility AI can bring, but she does not want to become technical to know whether the work is safe. The B Team has to show her where AI helps, where people stay responsible and where the system stops.

**Tweet.** The B Team makes AI credible by showing The Stop Line: approved proof, senior ownership and the clear limit the system will not cross. Every claim is traceable. Every serious promise is Signed by Humans.

## Key messages

The six-type Messaging Architecture — Awareness, Relevance, Emotion, Logic, Action, Commitment — under one umbrella message. Each message laddered with the Trident: 1° umbrella claim → 2° supporting pillar → 3° killer fact.
